findings.title: Anthropic: How Anthropic enables self-service data analytics with Claude (June 2026)
findings.what: Four layers: data foundations (a small set of canonical datasets, one repo for models, semantic layer and docs), ranked sources of truth (semantic layer > lineage graph > distilled query corpus > business context), skills (a knowledge skill that routes to about 30 domain reference files, plus a runbook skill with a dozen analysis patterns), and validation. Reported accuracy on their evals: at most 21% without skills, above 95% with skills. Giving the agent grep access to thousands of SQL files changed accuracy by less than one point, although about 80% of the missed questions had the answer in the corpus. Without maintenance, offline accuracy fell from about 95% to about 65% in one month; a code-review hook now flags model changes that do not touch a skill file (about 90% of data-model PRs include a skill change). An adversarial review step added 6% accuracy for 32% more tokens and 72% more latency. LLM-generated metric definitions were net-negative compared with a smaller human-curated layer.
findings.lesson: Access to raw material is not the bottleneck. Structure is: few canonical datasets, human-owned definitions, reference docs written for retrieval (grain, scope, exclusions, gotchas, routing triggers), and docs stored next to the code that produces the data so that one change updates both. Add a provenance footer to answers (source tier, freshness, owner). A sensible start is a few canonical datasets, a few dozen evals and one thin knowledge skill.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page (via WebFetch summary). The total size of the eval set and the warehouse are not given. All figures are self-reported by the vendor of the model, on internal evals.

findings.title: OpenAI: Inside our in-house data agent (Jan 2026) and the ByteByteGo interview with Emma Tang
findings.what: One LLM, a context assembly step, about 13 tools (cut from about 40) and a runtime, over 70k+ datasets and 600+ PB. Six context layers: table usage (schema, lineage, query history ranked by trust), human annotations, a nightly Codex job that reads the pipeline code of each table (100 to 200 tables per night, 5 to 10 minutes each), institutional knowledge (Slack, Docs, Notion, access-controlled), memory of corrections (global or personal scope), and live runtime queries when offline context is missing or stale. Layers 1 to 3 are merged offline, daily, into one description per table, which is embedded. Interfaces: Slack, web, IDE, Codex CLI via MCP.
findings.lesson: Put the complexity in offline curation (one dense, pre-built description per table) and keep the online loop simple. Embedding all historical queries failed; ranking queries by trustworthiness (dashboard queries first, one-off exploration last) worked. Overlapping tools gave conflicting answers, so no two tools should do the same job. Prompts that state the goal worked better than step-by-step prompts.
findings.verified: The OpenAI page returned 403; I could not read it. Details come from the ByteByteGo write-up of an interview (secondary, read in full via WebFetch) and from search snippets. The secondary sources disagree on scale (600 PB / 70k datasets in Jan 2026 versus 1.5 EB / 90k in May 2026) and on the model version. The memory figure (22 min --> 1 min 22 s) comes from a search snippet only. Evaluation method was not described in what I read.

findings.title: Vercel: We removed 80% of our agent's tools (d0, Dec 2025) and How to build agents with filesystems and bash (Jan 2026)
findings.what: d0, an internal text-to-SQL agent in Slack, replaced 17 specialised tools (schema search, join path finder, plan finalisers, validators...) by a bash tool in a sandbox plus SQL execution. The sandbox is loaded with the Cube semantic layer as a directory of YAML, Markdown and JSON files that the model explores with grep, cat, find and ls. On 5 representative queries: success 4/5 --> 5/5, average time 274.8 s --> 77.4 s, tokens about 102k --> 61k, steps about 12 --> 7. Model: Claude Opus 4.5.
findings.lesson: If the descriptions of the data are well-structured, consistently named files, a coding agent with a shell needs almost no custom retrieval tools. The authors state the condition themselves: with messy naming or undocumented joins, file access only gives faster bad queries. The work moves from tooling to documentation.
findings.verified: Both posts read on the primary pages. The benchmark is 5 queries, so the numbers are an anecdote, not a measurement with any statistical weight. The second post promotes Vercel's own bash-tool and sandbox.

findings.title: Pinterest: Unified Context-Intent Embeddings for Scalable Text-to-SQL (Analytics Agent, March 2026)
findings.what: 100k+ analytical tables, 2,500+ analysts. The catalog (PinCat, built on DataHub) holds tiers (Tier 1 strict docs, Tier 2 lighter, Tier 3 short retention), owners and glossary terms, and these governance fields enter the ranking of retrieved tables. Historical queries are enriched with catalog context, rewritten by an LLM into the analytical questions that they answer, then embedded; join keys, filters and aggregation patterns are extracted as reusable building blocks. Tools are exposed through MCP; validation checks that tables and columns exist, profiles column values (the 'WEB' versus 'web' case), runs EXPLAIN before execution and applies LIMIT 100. Explicit order when sources conflict: expert docs > catalog schema > query patterns > general knowledge.
findings.lesson: Declare a trust order between context sources, and show existing trusted assets before generating new SQL. Publish real values for categorical columns, because a query with a wrong literal runs without error and returns nothing. Governance metadata (tier, freshness, documentation completeness, owner) is useful to the agent as a ranking signal, not only to humans.
findings.verified: The Medium page returned 403. Details come from a third-party summary of the post (sysdesign-wiki, read in full) and from a DataHub recap of a Pinterest talk (vendor, read in full); the two agree. The post gives no accuracy figures and says that SQL generation 'has room for improvement'. Adoption (40% of analysts, 10x the next agent) is self-reported.

findings.title: Ramp: Meet Ramp Research, our agentic data analyst (Sept 2025)
findings.what: A Slack agent over a warehouse of thousands of tables. Context comes from indexed dbt, Looker and Snowflake metadata, plus technical documents written by the owner of each analytics domain and organised as a file system that the agent reads on demand. The agent can inspect column values, branch and backtrack. Evaluation moved from human review of each answer, to end-to-end tests, to a small Python framework inside the dbt project that asserts on intermediate steps (expected tool calls, tables referenced, query shape). 1,800+ questions, 300 users, 1,476 questions in four weeks against 66 in the human help channel. No access to PII.
findings.lesson: Tacit domain knowledge has to be written down by the people who own the domain, as files. Tests that check only the final answer do not say why an answer failed; asserting on which tables the agent used makes failures diagnosable. The loop is: edit context --> run tests --> confirm.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. A later dbt Labs recap of a dbt Summit 2026 talk (vendor blog, read) says volume reached 10,000 to 15,000 questions per month and that dashboards moved to SQL files in a repo that agents can edit; a search snippet says the agent became a coding agent in a sandbox, which I could not confirm on a page.

findings.title: Notion: How we built a personal data scientist for every Notion employee (Data Scout, Oct 2026)
findings.what: A Snowflake MCP connection where queries run under the Snowflake identity of each user, plus a Notion database used as a context index: one row per item with Title, Domain, Type (Skill, Metric Definition, Table Schema, FAQ), Keywords and Priority, with the details in the page body. The agent matches one or two domains first and reads only those bodies. A run_tagged_query wrapper appends metadata (metric, definition reference, context pages used, filters, time window) as a SQL comment. A nightly agent flags stale or conflicting context; a triage agent applies small fixes and escalates the rest. About half of employees use it; requests to the data team fell about 80% in two months.
findings.lesson: A small typed index with short descriptions, and bodies loaded on demand, worked better than putting all guidance in index properties. Tag each query with the definitions and context that produced it, so that answers can be traced afterwards. Pre-answer checks are about meaning (join duplication, numerator and denominator, completeness, one as-of date), because a query can run cleanly and answer the wrong question.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Notion sells the agent product described, so part of the post is promotion. Evals are stated as still in progress; the authors say that query success and usage do not prove accuracy.

findings.title: LinkedIn: Practical text-to-SQL for data analytics (SQL Bot, Dec 2024) and arXiv 2507.14372 (July 2025)
findings.what: Context sources: certified datasets with mandatory table descriptions written by domain experts, DataHub metadata (schema, top-K values of categorical fields, partition keys, deprecated flag), successful query logs (popularity, common joins), example queries from certified notebooks. Narrowing: popularity reduces millions of tables to thousands, embeddings give 20, an LLM re-ranker keeps 7; defaults are personalised from the org chart and access history. Validators check that tables and fields exist and run EXPLAIN; a 'Fix with AI' button accounts for about 80% of sessions. Benchmark: 130+ questions over 10 product areas. The later paper reports 300+ weekly users and 53% of responses correct or close to correct by expert review.
findings.lesson: Honest accuracy at warehouse scale is far from the 95% of survey satisfaction: 53% on their own benchmark. About 60% of benchmark questions needed several accepted answers, otherwise recall was under-reported by 10 to 15%. Top-K values per categorical field and a 'deprecated' flag in the metadata are cheap and high value.
findings.verified: Blog post read on the primary page; arXiv abstract read (not the full paper). The ablation figures from the Trino Summit slides (example queries: +16% table recall) come from a search snippet only.

findings.title: Uber: QueryGPT (Sept 2024)
findings.what: Started as plain RAG over schemas and SQL samples; accuracy declined as tables were added. The current design uses workspaces (12 curated collections of tables and SQL samples per business domain, plus custom ones), an intent agent that maps the question to a workspace, a table agent whose choice the user can confirm or edit, and a column prune agent (some schemas have 200+ columns, 40 to 60k tokens). Evaluation uses a golden set from real logs with intent, schemas and golden SQL, run in two flows: end-to-end, and 'decoupled' with the right tables supplied. About 300 daily users in a limited rollout.
findings.lesson: Narrow the search space by domain before any retrieval, and keep schemas small. Evaluate table selection and SQL generation separately, otherwise an upstream error hides the quality of the SQL step. The authors ignore run-to-run changes of about 5% because the model is non-deterministic: one eval run is a noisy measurement.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Design dates from 2023-2024 (32k context limits), so the column pruning matters less today; the evaluation design is still current.

findings.title: Uber: Unlocking financial insights with Finch (July 2025)
findings.what: A Slack agent for finance staff (LangGraph supervisor plus a SQL writer agent) that queries curated single-table data marts instead of the full warehouse. An OpenSearch index stores column names, column values, natural-language aliases for both ('US&C' --> US and Canada, 'GBs' --> gross bookings) and table-specific caveats. Role-based access is checked before execution. Evaluation compares results with golden queries, tests routing, and reruns historical queries before any prompt or model change.
findings.lesson: Wide, denormalised single tables remove the join problem and let the model fix its own errors quickly. An alias list for column values improves WHERE clauses more than schema plus sample rows. Compare outputs, not SQL text, because many queries give the same answer.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. No accuracy figures are published; the post says the agent 'is not 100% reliable and is prone to hallucination'.

findings.title: Grab: How AI is transforming analytics at Grab (Aug 2026)
findings.what: A Slack agent (Spartan) routes questions to 50+ skills and 120+ analysis frameworks and answers from certified metrics; context documents describe grain, exclusions and caveats. A context lifecycle manager proposes updates to context documents from instrumentation specs. An internal portal (BriX) lets teams assemble an app from a prompt, context files, a model and MCP connections, inheriting certified data and permissions. In one channel the share of threads answered fully by the agent rose from 53% to 67% (metric questions), 63% to 90% (data pulls), 50% to 81% (SQL requests).
findings.lesson: 'Ambiguous definitions cause most analytics slop': certify metrics at a stated grain first. Context goes stale quickly, so its maintenance must be part of the workflow. When the agent fails the same way twice, encode the fix in context, golden datasets, evals or gates.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. No accuracy measurement is given; the figures are shares of threads without analyst involvement, which is not the same as correct answers.

findings.title: Grab: Leveraging RAG-powered LLMs for analytical tasks (Data-Arks, Oct 2024)
findings.what: Instead of free text-to-SQL, Grab exposes frequently used, vetted SQL queries and Python functions as parameterised APIs (Data-Arks); any employee can upload one. An LLM selects the relevant API by retrieval, runs it and summarises the result in Slack (report summariser, fraud investigation bot). Reported saving: 3 to 4 hours per report.
findings.lesson: Most requests are the same query with different dates or filters. A library of vetted, parameterised queries gives exact answers for the common cases, and free SQL generation can be kept for the rest.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Older (2024) and no comparison with text-to-SQL is given.

findings.title: DataHub town hall recap (April 2026): Pinterest governance before the agent
findings.what: Pinterest reduced 400k+ mostly undocumented tables towards a curated base of about 100k. Before: about 500 ungoverned tables created per day, the top 500 tables carried 80% of query volume with almost no documentation, about 30% of the most-queried tables belonged to people who had left. Table creation now requires tier, owner, retention and domain, enforced at the metastore. LLM-drafted descriptions (75% rated usable or better) and propagation of glossary terms along join lineage (40%+ of in-scope columns) cut manual documentation work by about 70%.
findings.lesson: Make the metadata a condition of creating a dataset, so it cannot be skipped. LLM drafts with human review are acceptable for descriptions (compare with Anthropic: not for metric definitions). Regression checks on every commit to shared context.
findings.verified: Read on the page. It is a vendor recap of a customer talk; figures are self-reported and the only benchmark is qualitative.

patterns: Curate a small trusted subset instead of exposing the whole warehouse: canonical datasets (Anthropic), single-table marts (Uber Finch), workspaces (Uber QueryGPT), certified datasets (LinkedIn), tiers (Pinterest), certified metrics (Grab).

Context is built offline and served in dense form, and the online agent loop is kept simple with few tools: OpenAI (one description per table, 40 --> 13 tools), Vercel (17 tools --> bash plus SQL), Anthropic (skills as markdown folders).

Context as files that the agent reads on demand, with a small router or index on top: Anthropic (knowledge skill --> about 30 reference files), Vercel (semantic layer as YAML/Markdown), Ramp (domain documents as a file system), Notion (typed index, bodies on demand).

Raw query history does not help by itself; it has to be ranked or distilled: Anthropic (grep over the SQL corpus changed accuracy by less than one point), OpenAI (only trusted queries), Pinterest (queries rewritten as the questions that they answer), LinkedIn (certified notebooks, recency filters).

Humans own definitions and LLMs may draft descriptions: Anthropic (auto-generated metric definitions were net-negative), Ramp (domain owners write the docs), Pinterest (LLM drafts with human review per tier), Notion ('evidence is not approval').

Context decays fast and needs enforced maintenance: Anthropic (95% --> 65% in a month, CI hook), Notion (nightly review agent), Grab (context lifecycle manager), OpenAI (nightly enrichment, runtime checks for stale context), Pinterest (regression checks on commits to shared context).

Evaluation is a fixed set of questions with several accepted answers, checked on intermediate steps and rerun on every context change: Uber QueryGPT (decoupled flow, 5% noise band), LinkedIn (130+ questions, multiple valid answers), Ramp (assert on tables and tool calls), Anthropic (ablations, a few dozen evals per topic), Uber Finch (regression before prompt or model change).

Cheap validation before execution, and provenance after: table and column existence plus EXPLAIN (LinkedIn, Pinterest), value profiling for literals (Pinterest, Uber Finch aliases, LinkedIn top-K values), SQL and source tables returned with the answer (OpenAI), provenance footer (Anthropic), tagged queries (Notion). Permissions are passed through from the user's identity (Notion, Uber Finch, LinkedIn, OpenAI) and are not reimplemented in the agent.
disagreements: Semantic layer: required or not. Anthropic and Vercel put a compiled semantic layer first; Notion uses a library of pages and says it does not replace a semantic layer; OpenAI, LinkedIn and Pinterest work from enriched table descriptions and query history without one.

Retrieval: embeddings versus files and grep. OpenAI, Pinterest, LinkedIn and Uber (tens of thousands of tables and more) use vector or hybrid search. Vercel, Anthropic and Ramp (curated layers) let the agent read files. The split follows scale: nobody reports grep working over 100k tables, and nobody reports needing a vector store for a few dozen curated datasets.

Value of query history. Pinterest makes it the core asset and LinkedIn reports its largest recall gain from example queries (snippet only); Anthropic measured almost no gain from raw access to the corpus. The positions agree only if the history is distilled first.

Agent structure. Uber (QueryGPT, Finch) and LinkedIn use several narrow agents with routers (designs from 2023-2025); OpenAI, Vercel and Anthropic (2026) use one model with few tools and say that constraining the model's reasoning made results worse. This is probably an effect of model generation more than a real dispute.

LLM-written metadata. Pinterest and OpenAI generate table descriptions at scale (75% rated usable); Anthropic found LLM-generated metric definitions net-negative and three successive doc-refinement iterations net-negative. Descriptions and definitions are treated differently.

Reported accuracy is not comparable between sources. Anthropic reports about 95% on internal evals over a curated layer; LinkedIn reports 53% correct or close on its benchmark over a large lake, and 95% 'passes' in a user survey; Vercel's figures rest on 5 queries; OpenAI, Pinterest, Notion, Grab and Uber Finch publish no accuracy figure. Adoption counts are the common metric and they do not measure correctness.

Coverage gap of this search: the web search budget of the session ran out after six queries, so Meta, DoorDash, Airbnb, Shopify, Stripe, Netflix and Block Goose were not checked (pages returned 403 or no post was found on the index pages). Their absence here means 'not verified', not 'nothing published'.
results.for_adele: Adele already has the shape that these teams converged on: a dozen curated datasets, descriptors, a CLI plus SKILL.md, files read on demand. No vector store or semantic layer is needed at that size. Additions worth making: (1) per-dataset gotchas, exclusions, valid ranges and "use this dataset when..." routing lines, written by a human; (2) top-K values for categorical columns in `describe`; (3) descriptor stored and generated next to the fetch code, with a check that fails when one changes without the other; (4) a few dozen fixed questions with accepted answers, asserting on which datasets were used, rerun on every descriptor or skill change; (5) a few vetted parameterised example queries per dataset; (6) freshness and source printed with each query result.

findings.title: dbt Labs: Semantic Layer vs. Text-to-SQL, 2026 benchmark update
findings.what: dbt Labs (Ganz and Perigaud, 2026-04-07) reran the ACME Insurance benchmark: 11 questions, 20 runs each, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex. On the original normalized schema, raw text-to-SQL scored 64.5% and the semantic layer 72.7% overall. The semantic layer scored 100% on the questions inside its modeled scope and 0% on the questions that needed too many joins, where it returns an error. After an LLM wrote 3 extra dbt models, text-to-SQL rose to 90.0% / 84.1% and the semantic layer to 98.2% / 100%. Repo: github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-llm-sl-bench.
findings.lesson: Two results matter more than the headline. (1) Reshaping the tables (denormalized, well-named models) lifted raw SQL from about 64% to 84-90%, which is a larger gain than the semantic layer adds on top. (2) The two approaches fail differently: a semantic layer refuses when a question is out of scope, raw SQL returns a plausible wrong number. The evidence is thin: 11 questions on one schema, published by the vendor of the semantic layer, so the percentages are indicative and not precise.
findings.verified: Read the primary dbt blog page (all tables and the recommendation). Did not open the repo.

findings.title: Rumiantsau and Fokeev: Semantic Layers for Reliable LLM-Powered Data Analytics (arXiv 2604.25149)
findings.what: A paired benchmark (2026-04-28): 100 natural-language questions on the Contoso Retail dataset in ClickHouse, three models (Claude Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4), each question answered once with the schema only and once with the schema plus a 4 KB hand-written markdown document that describes measures, conventions and disambiguation rules. Accuracy rose from 45.5-50.5% to 67.7-68.7%, a gain of 17 to 23 points. The abstract states that the with/without difference is significant at p < 0.01 and that the three models are indistinguishable within each condition.
findings.lesson: The 'semantic layer' here is not a query engine. It is one short markdown file, and it explains more of the accuracy than the choice of model does. This is the closest published evidence for the position 'raw SQL plus good docs'. Limits: one dataset, 100 questions, single shot (no agent loop that can inspect data and retry), and the abstract does not name the statistical test, so treat 'indistinguishable' as 'no difference detected with 100 questions', not as 'equal'.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page only, not the full PDF.

findings.title: OpenAI: Inside our in-house data agent
findings.what: OpenAI describes an internal agent (GPT-5.2) for 3,500+ users over about 70,000 datasets and 600 PB. It has no classical semantic layer. It stacks six kinds of context: table usage and lineage from query history, human annotations, a Codex job that reads the pipeline code of each table (purpose, grain, keys, freshness, alternative tables), institutional knowledge from Slack/Docs/Notion, memory of saved corrections, and live queries at runtime. Evals are question / golden SQL pairs that run continuously like unit tests.
findings.lesson: Three stated lessons transfer directly: 'meaning lives in code' (the code that produces a table says more about grain, freshness and scope than the schema does), fewer and non-overlapping tools, and goal-level guidance instead of prescriptive steps. Also: a memory of corrections (non-obvious filters) and a small set of golden questions are part of the data layer, not extras.
findings.verified: The primary openai.com page returned 403. I read the full text through a mirror reader (hn.jakechampion.name), so content is the original article but not fetched from the primary host. No publication date visible. Secondary sources give conflicting scale numbers, I kept the ones in the article text.

findings.title: Vercel: We removed 80% of our agent's tools (d0)
findings.what: Vercel (Andrew Qu, 2025-12-22) replaced the specialised tools of its internal text-to-SQL agent with one bash tool in a sandbox. The agent reads the Cube semantic layer as a directory of YAML, Markdown and JSON files with grep, cat, find and ls (Claude Opus 4.5). On 5 representative queries: success 4/5 --> 5/5, average time 274.8 s --> 77.4 s, tokens about 102k --> 61k, steps about 12 --> 7.
findings.lesson: Semantic definitions can be consumed as plain files that the agent searches, without a semantic query API. The authors state the condition themselves: it worked because the files were already good documentation, and file access to a messy layer 'would only produce faster bad queries'. Five queries cannot support the 80% --> 100% success claim (one query changed outcome). The time and token reductions are the more credible part.
findings.verified: Read the primary Vercel blog page.

findings.title: a16z: Your Data Agents Need Context
findings.what: Investor essay (Cui and Li, 2026-03-10) that named the 'modern context layer' as a superset of the semantic layer. Five steps: access to all data, automated construction of context from query history / dbt / LookML, human refinement of tribal knowledge, exposure to agents by API or MCP, and flows that update the context when sources change or users correct answers. It splits the market into warehouse platforms (Databricks Genie, Snowflake Cortex Analyst), AI analyst companies and new context-layer companies.
findings.lesson: This is the reference framing that most 2026 vendor posts repeat. Its useful claim is that hand-built semantic layers go stale (its example: YAML written by a departed employee, missing two product lines), so the maintenance loop is the real design problem. It contains no measurements: it is a market thesis from an investor with portfolio interests.
findings.verified: Read the primary a16z page.

findings.title: Kaelio ktx: an open-source 'context layer' as files in git
findings.what: Apache-2.0 tool (about 1.6k stars) that ingests warehouses, dbt, LookML, Metabase and Notion into a git folder: semantic-layer/<connection>/ as YAML ('hard semantics' that compile to SQL) and wiki/ as Markdown ('soft semantics'). Agents use a CLI (ktx sl, ktx wiki, ktx sql as read-only escape hatch, ktx sl validate against the live schema), an MCP server and an installable skill. Supports DuckDB among 10 databases. The companion blog post (Simon Spaeti, 2026-06-04) explains the hard/soft split.
findings.lesson: The closest existing project to a CLI + skill + descriptor design. Ideas worth copying: split executable definitions (YAML) from interpretive notes (Markdown), keep both in git and reviewed like code, validate descriptors against the live schema, and keep a read-only raw SQL path next to the governed path. No accuracy numbers are published in the repo, and the blog's 'faster and more correct' claim rests on a screenshot.
findings.verified: Read the GitHub README and the Kaelio blog post (https://www.kaelio.com/blog/building-a-context-layer-for-the-agentic-era). The claim of rank 1 on Spider 2.0-Lite is the vendor's and not checked.

findings.title: Apache Ossie (incubating), formerly Open Semantic Interchange
findings.what: Vendor-neutral YAML/JSON specification for exchanging semantic models: datasets, fields, relationships, metrics, plus an ai_context element (instructions, synonyms, examples) at model, field and metric level and custom_extensions per vendor. Started by Snowflake, dbt Labs, Salesforce and BI vendors in 2025, entered the Apache Incubator and was renamed on 2026-07-10. Released spec is 0.1.1, drafts are 0.2.0 / 0.3.0.dev0. Apache Polaris has a beta Semantic Model API that stores Ossie documents. Converters exist for Snowflake semantic views and dbt.
findings.lesson: The industry is converging on a descriptor file with a dedicated field for agent instructions, which validates 'descriptor + agent notes' as a design. But Ossie is an interchange format, not a runtime, and a reviewer (Alex Merced, 2026-08-25) lists what it lacks: no fields for ownership, freshness, lineage or provenance, no portable expression language, no discovery of the model for a given table. Frictionless already covers freshness and provenance better. Borrow the ai_context idea, do not adopt the unstable spec.
findings.verified: Read ossie.apache.org and the independent write-up https://datalakehousehub.com/blog/apache-ossie-polaris-semantic-models. Did not read the spec file itself. Participant counts (17 founders, 50+ backers) come from secondary pages.

findings.title: Andy Chen: The Enterprise Context Layer (markdown in git, written by agents)
findings.what: Essay (2026-03-10) from a company of about 1,000 people: 20 parallel agents ran for about two days and produced 1,020 markdown files in 11 domains (about 6,000 commits) with about 1,000 lines of Python. Every claim needs an inline citation, conflicts between sources are documented instead of resolved, and folders plus backlinks replace the ontology and the graph database. A derived open implementation adds AGENTS.md, per-domain SKILL.md files, staleness windows and a tiered ranking of source authority.
findings.lesson: The 'files in a repo, no semantic layer, no graph' position in its pure form. Transferable rules: cite the source of every statement in a context file, record conflicts, give each kind of fact an expiry window, rank sources (code above chat). The evidence is anecdotal: the author judges accuracy against his own understanding, gives no error rates, and has not yet built the query interface.
findings.verified: Read the primary Substack essay and the derived tutorial at https://tmfnk.pages.dev/use/tutorials/the-enterprise-context-layer/.

findings.title: Snowflake semantic views and Databricks metric views (semantics as warehouse objects)
findings.what: Both warehouses now store semantics as first-class catalog objects. Snowflake semantic views hold logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions and metrics, are created by SQL, YAML or an 'Autopilot' wizard that imports Tableau / Power BI files, and are attached to Cortex Agents as a tool. Databricks metric views (YAML, Unity Catalog) hold measures, dimensions, joins and 'agent metadata' (synonyms, display names, formats), with a beta feature that declares relationships so that assistants choose the right join path.
findings.lesson: The platform position is 'semantic layer inside the engine, queried with SQL, annotated for agents'. The agent-specific additions are modest and cheap to imitate in any descriptor: synonyms, display names, declared join paths, and generation of the first draft from existing artifacts. Neither page gives accuracy evidence.
findings.verified: Read the Snowflake overview page and the Databricks page https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/metric-views/. The 57% --> 78% BIRD figure attributed to Snowflake comes from a search snippet of an Atlan page and is not verified.

findings.title: Sequeda, Allemang, Jacob: knowledge graph benchmark for question answering on enterprise SQL (arXiv 2311.07509)
findings.what: The 2023 paper behind most 'ontology / knowledge graph' claims and the origin of the ACME Insurance dataset that dbt reuses. GPT-4, zero-shot: 16% accuracy on the SQL schema directly, 54% when questions are answered over a knowledge graph built from an ontology and mappings.
findings.lesson: The ontology position rests mainly on this old result with one model. The dbt rerun shows the raw SQL baseline on the same dataset rose to about 64% by 2026 and to 84-90% after simple remodeling, so the advantage of a formal ontology over 'better tables plus descriptions' is no longer demonstrated. I found no 2026 head-to-head test of ontology versus markdown docs.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page. Comparison with 2026 numbers is my inference from the dbt post, not a claim of the paper.

findings.title: Bodo PyDough: 100% on dbt's benchmark without hand-built models
findings.what: Bodo (2026-09-09) reports 220/220 correct runs on the 11 dbt questions. Offline, it derives a metadata graph from the schema, profiles every column with SQL, renders the statistics as English and adds one LLM summary per column. Online, it generates several candidates and takes the consensus (about 11 LLM calls, 1.5 cents per question). It replaced dbt's harness with a local SQLite copy.
findings.lesson: Automatic column profiling (value ranges, distinct values, null rates, rendered as text) can substitute for a part of hand modeling. A fixed pipeline with voting, with no exploring agent, is enough on a small schema. Not a controlled comparison: different execution setup, the same 11 questions, vendor-run and not validated by dbt.
findings.verified: Read the primary Bodo post.

findings.title: TextQL: Semantic Layers Are a Patch. Ontologies Are the Fix.
findings.what: TextQL (2026-05-26) argues that semantic layers are accurate inside their modeled scope but that coverage grows only with engineering headcount. It cites BIRD (about 82% for top systems with column hints, 93% for humans), LiveSQLBench (42% for Gemini 3.1 Pro on unmodeled data) and the dbt 0% out-of-scope result. Its 'ontology' is in practice git-controlled files of documentation plus structured .tql definitions that agents navigate.
findings.lesson: Note the vocabulary drift: this 'ontology' is a folder of docs and definitions in git, close to ktx and to the markdown position, not an OWL graph. The coverage argument against semantic layers is sound and agrees with dbt's own data. The efficiency claims (7x faster, 24x less compute) have no methodology.
findings.verified: Read the primary TextQL post. Did not check the BIRD and LiveSQLBench leaderboards.

findings.title: MotherDuck: Context, Semantics, and Ontology primer
findings.what: A definitional essay (mid 2026, apparently by Simon Spaeti) that separates semantic layer (logic that compiles to SQL, deterministic metrics), context layer (rules and unstructured knowledge, continuously updated), ontology (object types, links, properties) and context graph. It recommends semantic plus context layer together, a graph only when the domain is interconnected enough, and says that MotherDuck's own evals found that a graph approach 'picked worse', without figures.
findings.lesson: A useful decision rule: choose by the cost of a wrong answer and by who consumes the output. Outputs that feed dashboards or scheduled jobs need deterministic definitions, outputs that feed a reasoning agent with a human checkpoint can rely on docs. 'A flat index of guide titles can be enough.' Governance of context (who updates it, how stale it is) is named as the hard part, with a proposed quality score per context item.
findings.verified: Read the primary page. Author and date are inferred from links, not stated. The eval remark has no numbers.

findings.title: dbt agent skills and Palantir Ontology MCP (how incumbents expose their layer to agents)
findings.what: dbt Labs ships its agent interface as a repo of Agent Skills (762 stars), among them building-dbt-semantic-layer, answering-natural-language-questions-with-dbt, running-dbt-commands and querying-the-dbt-information-schema, next to an MCP server. Palantir exposes its ontology in two ways: Palantir MCP for builders (edit ontology types) and Ontology MCP for consumers, which turns object types, action types and query functions into MCP tools with per-application restrictions.
findings.lesson: Even the vendors of semantic layers and ontologies now deliver SKILL.md folders plus a CLI or MCP as the agent interface. The skill tells the agent the procedure (check the governed layer first, fall back to SQL), the layer supplies the definitions. Palantir's distinctive element is typed actions (writes), which a read-only data layer does not need.
findings.verified: Read the GitHub README of dbt-agent-skills and the Palantir docs page https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/palantir-mcp/overview. Did not read individual skill files.

patterns: Written descriptions of the data explain more accuracy than the choice of model: a 4 KB markdown file adds 17-23 points (Rumiantsau and Fokeev), and modeling adds 20-25 points to raw SQL (dbt Labs).

The 'context layer' is framed as a superset of the semantic layer: executable definitions (YAML/SQL) plus prose knowledge (Markdown), usually auto-drafted and then refined by humans (a16z, Kaelio ktx, MotherDuck primer, OpenAI).
Context is stored as files in git and reviewed like code, and agents read it with file tools or a CLI instead of a dedicated semantic API (Vercel d0, ktx, Andy Chen, TextQL, dbt agent skills).

Context is generated from existing artifacts instead of written by hand: pipeline code (OpenAI), query history and BI files (a16z, Snowflake Autopilot), column profiling (Bodo PyDough), agents that read company sources (Andy Chen).

Hybrid routing is the common recommendation: governed metrics when the number must be exact, raw read-only SQL with rich schema context for exploration (dbt Labs, ktx escape hatch, MotherDuck primer).

Maintenance is named as the hard part, not creation: staleness, ownership, memory of corrections and continuous evals with golden SQL (OpenAI, a16z, MotherDuck primer, Andy Chen, Merced on Ossie's missing trust fields).
Fewer, more general tools and goal-level guidance work better with current models than many specialised tools and prescriptive prompts (OpenAI, Vercel).

Agent-specific annotations are being added to descriptor formats: ai_context with instructions, synonyms and examples (Apache Ossie), agent metadata and declared join paths (Databricks metric views), semantic views as agent tools (Snowflake).
disagreements: Semantic layer required versus docs sufficient: dbt Labs shows 98-100% with a semantic layer, but its own data shows raw SQL at 84-90% once tables are remodeled, and the arXiv paper gets its whole gain from a markdown file. No source compares 'semantic layer engine' against 'same information as prose' on the same questions.

Refusal versus coverage: a semantic layer scores 0% outside its modeled scope but never returns a wrong number (dbt). TextQL and a16z count this as the fatal limit (coverage grows with headcount), dbt counts it as the main safety property.

Ontology / knowledge graph versus plain files: Sequeda et al. (2023, GPT-4) show 16% --> 54% with a knowledge graph, Palantir and TextQL build on ontologies, while Andy Chen and the MotherDuck primer argue that folders and backlinks suffice and MotherDuck reports (without numbers) that a graph performed worse. The 2023 baseline is outdated and there is no 2026 head-to-head test.
The word 'ontology' is used for different things: typed objects and actions at Palantir, an OWL-style graph in Sequeda et al., git files of docs and definitions at TextQL.

Hand-curated versus auto-generated context: a16z's example is a hand-built layer that went stale, Bodo and OpenAI generate context automatically, while Vercel says that its result depended on a layer that was already well curated.

Evidence quality is weak across the whole debate: benchmarks have 5 (Vercel), 11 (dbt, Bodo) or 100 (arXiv) questions on one schema each, and most are run by a vendor of the winning approach. With so few questions, one changed outcome moves the score by 9 to 20 points, so differences of that size between approaches are not established.
Whether a standard descriptor matters: Ossie has 50+ backers but an unstable 0.x spec, no runtime, and no freshness or provenance fields, and most tools do not yet import it directly.

Coverage limits of this search: the web search budget ran out after five queries, so Malloy, LookML/Looker, Cube's own agent features, Timbr, GraphRAG over schemas, Anthropic's internal analytics write-up, Buster, Honeydew and AGENTS.md conventions for data were not checked on primary pages.
results.for_adele: Adele's design (descriptor + CLI + SKILL.md, raw DuckDB SQL) matches the best-supported position for a dozen clean tables: no semantic engine is needed. The evidence says to invest in (1) table shape: wide, well-named, pre-joined Parquet, (2) one short prose file per dataset with grain, conventions, known traps and disambiguation rules, with its source cited, (3) automatic column profiles in `describe` (ranges, distinct values, nulls), (4) an Ossie-like `ai_context` field (synonyms, example queries) inside the Frictionless descriptor, (5) a file of saved corrections, (6) ten to twenty golden question/SQL pairs run as tests. Keep few tools. Add governed metrics only if a number must be exact.

findings.title: Supporting Our AI Overlords: Redesigning Data Systems to be Agent-First (UC Berkeley, arXiv 2509.00997, CIDR 2026)
findings.what: The paper names the agent workload "agentic speculation": a high volume of exploratory queries, characterised by scale, heterogeneity, redundancy and steerability. Case studies: the success rate rises with the number of attempts (by 14% to 70%), only 10 to 20% of the sub-plans across 50 attempts are distinct, and traces start with metadata and sample rows, then statistics, then the solution. Giving "grounding hints" (for example which column matters) reduced SQL queries per trace from 12.67 to 10.38 (18.1%) and partial-query attempts by 36.6%. Proposed architecture: probes (SQL plus a natural-language brief), a probe optimizer that returns approximate answers during exploration, an agentic memory store, and side information such as related tables and cost estimates.
findings.lesson: An agent explores before it answers: metadata first, then sample rows, then statistics. A layer that serves those three steps cheaply and in few tokens (a compact describe, pre-computed column statistics, hints on which column to use) removes a measurable share of the exploratory queries. Catalog dumps of thousands of rows waste the context window, so describe output must be filtered and small.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv HTML v2 through WebFetch (model-summarised extraction of the primary page); the numbers quoted come from that extraction. The CIDR 2026 PDF was not opened.

findings.title: Databricks: How agentic software development will change databases (Lakebase / Neon)
findings.what: Post of 2026-03-30 by Pandis, Shamgunov and Xin. Claims from Lakebase telemetry: agents create about 4x more databases than humans, a project has about 10 branches on average, some branch trees are more than 500 levels deep, and for about half of the agentic applications the database compute lives less than 10 seconds. Derived requirements: O(1) copy-on-write branching, no monthly cost floor, scale to zero with sub-second start, and standard Postgres interfaces and error messages because agents already know them. A companion post (2026-04-29) says an agent can provision a Neon database through the Stripe Projects CLI "in under 350ms".
findings.lesson: The vendors with the best telemetry describe agent workloads as small, short-lived, bursty and mostly discarded. The consequences are: make creation and disposal nearly free, make idle cost zero, and keep the interface a dialect that the model already knows (plain Postgres here; DuckDB SQL plays that role for an embedded analytical layer).
findings.verified: Both Databricks posts read through WebFetch. The numbers are vendor telemetry, not independently checked. The older "80% of Neon databases are created by agents" figure appears only in search snippets (attributed to Ghodsi via Axios) and was not found on the Neon agents page that I fetched.

findings.title: Databricks Genie: best practices for curating an agent over tables
findings.what: The official guidance says to keep the scope narrow: "Aim for five or fewer tables", with a hard limit of 50 tables, views or metric views, and to pre-join or denormalise into views or metric views. Table and column descriptions in Unity Catalog are called "critical" for accuracy. Instructions have a priority order: SQL expressions for business terms, then example SQL, and "text instructions only as a last resort". Reviewed questions become benchmark questions, and the agent definition can be versioned as code.
findings.lesson: The most detailed vendor advice is about curation, not about the engine: few wide denormalised tables, hidden confusing columns, good column descriptions, worked example queries ahead of prose rules, and a small set of benchmark questions that is rerun after each change.
findings.verified: Docs page read through WebFetch. No accuracy numbers are given on the page; the advice is prescriptive, not measured.

findings.title: Snowflake-managed MCP server and semantic views
findings.what: The MCP server is a schema-level object defined in SQL. It exposes six tool types (Cortex Agent, coding agent, Cortex Search, Cortex Analyst, SQL execution, generic UDF or procedure), at most 50 tools per server, tool responses truncated at 250 KB, and only the tools part of MCP (no resources, prompts or sampling). Cortex Analyst over MCP works only with semantic views (logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions, metrics), not with the older YAML semantic models. Access to the server does not grant access to the tools, tool annotations are "client-facing hints, not security controls", and exposing raw SQL next to an agent lets the client bypass the agent's governance.
findings.lesson: Snowflake moved the semantic description from a side file into a first-class object of the database and made it the only route for natural-language queries. It also caps the size of a tool response and puts enforcement in roles, not in tool descriptions. For a small layer: hard-cap the output size, and make read-only a property of the connection, not a sentence in the instructions.
findings.verified: Snowflake docs for the managed MCP server and for the semantic view overview read through WebFetch. The launch blog post returned HTTP 403, so the launch date (October 2025) comes from search snippets only.

findings.title: BigQuery remote MCP server, MCP Toolbox for Databases, and conversational analytics data agents
findings.what: The managed BigQuery MCP server (preview announced 2026-01-08) has six tools: list_dataset_ids, list_table_ids, get_dataset_info, get_table_info, execute_sql and execute_sql_readonly. Queries are cancelled after three minutes and results are capped at 3,000 rows; the docs recommend a separate identity for agents. The open-source MCP Toolbox (googleapis/genai-toolbox, about 16.9k stars, v1.17.0) instead lets the owner define tools as parameterised SQL in a tools.yaml and group them in toolsets. BigQuery data agents take knowledge sources (at most 100, advice to split above 20), descriptions, glossary terms and "verified queries", with the stated priority: verified queries, then glossary, then instructions.
findings.lesson: The managed surface converges on the same four verbs as a list | describe | query CLI, with a separate read-only query tool and fixed row and time caps. Two styles coexist: free SQL with caps (managed server) and pre-written parameterised queries (Toolbox). Verified queries rank above prose instructions here too.
findings.verified: The Google Cloud blog post, the BigQuery MCP docs, the conversational analytics docs and the genai-toolbox README were each read through WebFetch. The blog post has no tool names; they come from the docs page.

findings.title: ClickHouse: Building a data platform for agents, and clickhousectl
findings.what: Post of 2026-07-30 by Al Brown. It claims that agents produce bursts of concurrent low-latency queries and need discoverability, documentation readable by an LLM, and "short-lived, task-scoped permissions". Shipped: an open-source MCP server that is read-only by default (it also queries local files through chDB), open-source Agent Skills with prioritised best practices, llms.txt and Markdown versions of every blog post, AGENTS.md support, and a one-command local stack. Internal assistant DWAINE: more than 250 users, about 70% of warehouse questions handled. A separate CLI (clickhousectl, beta 2026-04-09) gives JSON output on every command and installs skill files into more than fifteen coding agents.
findings.lesson: An analytical database vendor now ships the same three artefacts as a small self-hosted layer: a CLI with JSON output, skill files that carry the usage knowledge, and a read-only default. Documentation served as Markdown is treated as part of the product for agents.
findings.verified: The ClickHouse blog post was read through WebFetch. The clickhousectl details come from an analyst article (Futurum, 2026-04-15), not from ClickHouse's own page; the article quotes ClickHouse as "still investigating what good looks like for agent guardrails". The ClickHouse docs page on agentic analytics contains no workload numbers, contrary to a search snippet ("dozens of SQL queries per question"), which I could not confirm.

findings.title: Tiger Data: Agentic Postgres (Postgres for Agents)
findings.what: Launch post of 2025-10-21 by Kulkarni and Freedman. Stated differences: "Agents don't click, they call", "Agents don't remember, they retrieve", agents parallelise, need a sandbox, and can overload infrastructure and budget. Shipped: an MCP server with built-in prompts for schema design, query tuning and migrations plus search over the Postgres docs, copy-on-write forks of a whole database on a new block store (Fluid Storage, more than 110,000 IOPS per volume), BM25 and vector search inside Postgres, a CLI and a free tier.
findings.lesson: The MCP server carries expertise (how to design and tune), not only access. That is the same idea as a SKILL.md: the layer should teach the agent how to use it well, because the agent retrieves knowledge at each session instead of remembering it.
findings.verified: Launch post read through WebFetch. It is a product announcement; the IOPS figure is the vendor's own benchmark. InfoQ coverage (December 2025) seen in snippets only.

findings.title: Microsoft Fabric data agent (concept and limits)
findings.what: A generally available agent that selects among at most five data sources (lakehouse, warehouse, Power BI semantic model, KQL database, ontology, Microsoft Graph), then generates SQL, DAX or KQL, validates it and runs it. It is strictly read-only, runs with the identity of the requesting user, accepts instructions and up to 100 example queries per source, and caps answers at 25 rows and 25 columns. Lakehouse files (CSV, JSON) are not readable until they are exposed as tables. The docs state a precedence order: organisation policy, then role, then developer instructions, then user prompt.
findings.lesson: Microsoft bounds the agent tightly: few sources, selected tables only, small answers, read-only by construction, and a declared order of precedence between policy and instructions. The 25-row cap shows the design target: answers and aggregates, not exports. A layer that also needs bulk data needs a separate path for it (a pull command to a file).
findings.verified: Full Microsoft Learn page read through WebFetch (page updated 2026-10-21). Fabric IQ and ontology details were not researched beyond the mention on this page.

findings.title: Databricks managed MCP servers under Unity Catalog
findings.what: Databricks exposes Genie, SQL, vector search and Unity Catalog functions as MCP endpoints. The newer ones (system.ai.genie_one_mcp, system.ai.dbsql, sandbox, web search) are Unity Catalog securables called through a gateway that adds grants, policies and tracing tables; the older workspace endpoints "bypass Unity Gateway" and rely only on the permissions of the underlying objects. Queries run under the permissions of the caller.
findings.lesson: The tool itself becomes a governed and logged catalog object. The transferable part for a small system is the trace: log every agent query with the caller and the dataset, because that log is both the audit record and the evidence for which descriptions and examples need work.
findings.verified: Docs page read through WebFetch. Several of the listed servers are marked Beta or Public Preview on the page. Agent Bricks was not researched (search budget exhausted).

findings.title: MotherDuck remote MCP server (docs)
findings.what: The managed server is read-write by default (a separate guide covers a read-only restriction). It groups tools for querying, schema exploration, catalog search and documentation questions, plus saved artefacts (Dives, Flights) and "Guides": Markdown documents with metric definitions and join conventions that the agent reads. For clients that support MCP instructions it sends DuckDB query guidelines. The docs state that "every tool result the MCP server returns passes through the model's context" and recommend the CLI to agents that have a shell for exporting large results.
findings.lesson: A vendor that sells an MCP server tells shell-capable agents to use the CLI for anything large, because MCP results cost context tokens. Guides stored next to the data (metric definitions, join conventions) are the same device as descriptor notes plus a SKILL.md.
findings.verified: Docs page read through WebFetch. The page gives no row limits or timeouts and names only two tools explicitly. The earlier search already covered MotherDuck; only the points on token cost and Guides are new here.

findings.title: Supabase MCP server: security guidance
findings.what: The docs recommend read-only mode (SQL runs as a read-only Postgres user), scoping the server to one project, enabling only the needed tool groups, working on a branch, and connecting to production "only when the task requires production evidence". Supabase wraps SQL results with text that discourages the model from following instructions found in the data, and says: "This is not foolproof".
findings.lesson: Query results are untrusted text that enters the model. Read-only access prevents writes but not a leak through the model's own answer. For public datasets the leak risk is low, but free-text columns fetched from the web can still carry instructions, so the output format should mark data clearly as data.
findings.verified: Docs page read through WebFetch. The fetched page itself contained an embedded instruction addressed to AI readers (send a feedback report to Supabase); it was ignored, and it illustrates the point.

findings.title: Intelligence is Free, Now What? Data Systems for, of, and by Agents (BAIR blog)
findings.what: Perspective piece of 2026-07-07 by Parameswaran and eleven co-authors (including Zaharia, Hellerstein, Stoica). It repeats the 10 to 20% distinct sub-plans result and says that redundancy still improves success, so the aim is to make it cheap (shared scans, approximate answers, batched queries, latency estimates), not to remove it. It argues that Markdown files plus grep will not scale as agent memory and proposes structured memory keyed by table, column and type of operation, holding corrections instead of raw traces. It also reports engines generated by agents for one workload in minutes to hours for a few dollars.
findings.lesson: Do not try to stop the agent from issuing many small queries; make each one fast and cheap (local Parquet and DuckDB already do). Notes learned from use ("this column is in local time", "this join duplicates rows") are most useful when attached to the table and column they concern, which a per-dataset descriptor can hold.
findings.verified: Blog post read through WebFetch. It is a position piece; the follow-up papers it links (arXiv 2602.13521, 2603.02001, 2603.02081) were not opened.

findings.title: DoltHub: Agents Need Branches (response to the Berkeley paper) and Turso AgentFS
findings.what: Tim Sehn (2025-09-24) argues that agents that write need Git-style branches with per-statement rollback and inspectable diffs, since long MVCC transactions only offer all-or-nothing rollback. He quotes the paper's figure that agents "created 20x more branches, and performed 50x more rollbacks, relative to humans" and notes that its source (a Neon web page) is unclear. Turso's AgentFS (2025-11-13, https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs) takes a different route: one SQLite file per agent holds a POSIX-like filesystem, a key-value store and an append-only log of tool calls, so a snapshot is a file copy.
findings.lesson: Branching, forks and snapshots answer the problem of agents that write. A layer where agents only read published datasets does not need them. The useful residue is versioning of the data itself (a dated snapshot per fetch) so that an agent's result can be reproduced, and an append-only log of what the agent ran.
findings.verified: Both posts read through WebFetch. The 20x and 50x figures are quoted second-hand from the paper and the post itself questions their source.

patterns: Agent workloads are described the same way by researchers and vendors: many small exploratory queries in bursts, mostly redundant and mostly discarded, with metadata exploration first (Berkeley Agent-First paper, BAIR blog, ClickHouse, Databricks Lakebase post).

The surface converges on a few verbs (list, describe, query, plus a read-only variant of query) with fixed caps on rows, bytes and time: BigQuery MCP (3,000 rows, 3 minutes), Snowflake MCP (250 KB, 50 tools), Fabric data agent (25 rows by 25 columns).

Curated context is the main accuracy lever and example queries rank above prose instructions: Databricks Genie (SQL expressions, then example SQL, text last), BigQuery data agents (verified queries, then glossary, then instructions), Fabric (up to 100 example queries per source), Snowflake (semantic views).
Narrow scope beats wide access: Genie advises five or fewer tables, BigQuery advises splitting above 20 sources, Fabric allows five sources and selected tables only.
Semantics move into first-class database objects next to the data instead of side files: Snowflake semantic views, Databricks metric views, MotherDuck Guides, BigQuery glossary terms.

Read-only is the default and is enforced by identity and roles, not by tool descriptions: ClickHouse MCP, Supabase read-only user, Fabric, BigQuery execute_sql_readonly, Snowflake (annotations are hints, not controls).

Vendors ship usage knowledge with the access path, as skills, prompts or Markdown docs, and add a CLI with JSON output beside MCP: ClickHouse Agent Skills and clickhousectl, Tiger MCP prompts and CLI, MotherDuck query guidelines and CLI advice, Stripe Projects CLI for Neon.

For agents that write, the answer is cheap isolation and disposal: copy-on-write branches or forks, scale to zero, snapshots (Databricks Lakebase and Neon, Tiger Fluid Storage, DoltHub, Turso AgentFS).
disagreements: Free SQL with caps (BigQuery execute_sql_readonly, ClickHouse MCP, MotherDuck) versus mediated access where the agent never writes raw SQL against tables (Snowflake Cortex Analyst over semantic views, MCP Toolbox parameterised tools). Snowflake's own docs warn that exposing raw SQL beside an agent bypasses its governance.

Reduce redundant agent queries or accept them: the Berkeley paper shows that hints cut queries by about 18%, yet the BAIR post says redundancy raises success and should be made cheap, not removed. Rough approximate answers can also backfire by triggering more follow-up queries.
MCP versus CLI is not settled inside single vendors: MotherDuck and ClickHouse ship both and steer shell-capable agents to the CLI for large outputs; the hyperscalers ship managed MCP only.

The headline numbers are weak evidence. They are vendor telemetry (4x databases, 10-second compute lifetime, 350 ms provisioning), the 80% Neon figure exists only second-hand, and DoltHub notes that the paper's 20x branches and 50x rollbacks trace back to an unclear Neon web page. A search snippet claiming "dozens of SQL queries per question" for ClickHouse was not on the page when fetched.
Read-write by default (MotherDuck remote MCP, Supabase unless configured) versus read-only by default (ClickHouse, Fabric).

Coverage limit of this search: the shared web search budget ran out after six queries, so the remaining sources were fetched from known URLs. Not covered: Agent Bricks, Fabric IQ ontologies, Open Semantic Interchange, Turso beyond AgentFS, Postgres MCP Pro, Snowflake Cortex Agents internals.
results.for_adele: Adele's shape (list | describe | query | pull, read-only, descriptors, SKILL.md) matches what the platforms converged on. Branching, forks and scale to zero solve problems of agents that write; Adele can skip them. Worth adding: (1) hard caps on rows, bytes and time for query, with pull as the path for bulk data; (2) verified example queries per dataset in the descriptor, ranked above prose notes; (3) pre-computed column statistics in describe, since agents explore metadata, samples, then statistics; (4) few wide denormalised views instead of many tables; (5) a small set of benchmark questions rerun after each change; (6) an append-only query log; (7) a dated snapshot per fetch for reproducibility; (8) clear marking of result text as data.

findings.title: Vercel + Braintrust: "Testing if bash is all you need" (SQL vs bash vs filesystem vs hybrid agents on the same data)
findings.what: Ankur Goyal (Braintrust) and Andrew Qu (Vercel), 2026-01-22. Four agents answer questions on a dataset of GitHub issues and pull requests: SQL on SQLite, bash (just-bash) over about 68,000 JSON files, plain search/read file tools, and a hybrid of bash + SQLite. SQL: 100% accuracy, about 156k tokens, $0.51, 45 s. Bash: 52.7%, about 1.06M tokens, $3.34, 401 s. File tools: 63.0%, about 1.28M tokens, $3.89. Hybrid: 100% after fixes, at about 2x the tokens of SQL, because the agent checked SQL results against the files with grep. Five expected answers in the benchmark were wrong and had to be corrected.
findings.lesson: For tabular data with a clear schema, a SQL interface is far cheaper and more accurate than files explored with grep/cat. Files are useful next to SQL (for schema and documentation, and to spot-check results), not instead of it. Also: the benchmark itself had errors, so read the traces before trusting a score.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Number of questions and number of repeated runs not reported in what I read, so the uncertainty on the percentages is unknown.

findings.title: Vercel d0: "We removed 80% of our agent's tools" (file system agent over a semantic layer)
findings.what: Andrew Qu, 2025-12-22. The internal text-to-SQL agent d0 went from 17 specialised tools (schema lookup, query validation, error recovery) to two: bash in a Vercel Sandbox plus ExecuteSQL. The agent explores a Cube semantic layer stored as YAML, Markdown and JSON files with ls/grep/cat/find, using Claude Opus 4.5. On 5 queries: success 4/5 --> 5/5, mean time 274.8 s --> 77.4 s, tokens about 102k --> 61k, steps about 12 --> 7.
findings.lesson: The pattern is 'documentation as files + one SQL tool', not 'data as files'. The authors say it worked only because the semantic layer was already well-named and documented ("otherwise you just get faster bad queries"). The evidence is weak: with 5 queries, one query that flips changes the success rate by 20 points, so 80% versus 100% cannot be distinguished from chance. The time and token reductions are large enough to be more credible.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page (numbers, stack, caveats). No repeated runs or variance reported.

findings.title: Anthropic: "Introducing advanced tool use" (tool search, programmatic tool calling, tool use examples)
findings.what: 2025-11-24. Three API features with internal measurements. Tool search (definitions loaded on demand): context for 50+ MCP tools from about 77k to 8.7k tokens, accuracy on MCP evaluations 49% --> 74% (Opus 4) and 79.5% --> 88.1% (Opus 4.5). Programmatic tool calling (the model writes code that calls tools in a sandbox, intermediate results stay out of context): mean tokens 43,588 --> 27,297 (-37%), accuracy 25.6% --> 28.5% on internal retrieval and 46.5% --> 51.2% on GAIA. Tool use examples: 72% --> 90% on complex parameter handling.
findings.lesson: This is the best-quantified vendor evidence that (a) loading descriptions on demand and (b) letting the agent filter data in code before it sees it both save tokens and do not hurt accuracy. The large accuracy gain is for on-demand discovery with many tools; the gain from code execution is mostly tokens. Concrete usage examples in a tool or command description have a large measured effect.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. All figures are Anthropic internal tests, sample sizes not given.

findings.title: Anthropic "Code execution with MCP" and Cloudflare "Code Mode" (tools presented as a code API in a file tree)
findings.what: Anthropic (2025-11-04, https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp) proposes a servers/ directory with one file per tool that the agent lists and reads on demand, and data filtered in the execution environment (the model sees 5 of 10,000 rows). Its 150,000 --> 2,000 tokens (98.7%) figure is one worked example with no method given. Cloudflare (Matt Carey, 2026-02-20) ships an MCP server for its whole API (2,500+ endpoints) with two tools, search() and execute(): the agent writes JavaScript against the OpenAPI spec inside a V8 isolate, about 1,000 tokens of definitions versus 1.17M tokens for one tool per endpoint.
findings.lesson: A fixed, tiny interface (search the catalogue with code, then execute) scales with the size of the catalogue, where one tool per object does not. The costs: you need a sandbox, and the token figures count definitions only, not what a session consumes. Neither post measures task accuracy.
findings.verified: Both primary pages read. The Cloudflare page gives two different baselines (over 2M in the summary, 1.17M measured with tiktoken in the body). The Anthropic 98.7% is illustrative, not a benchmark.

findings.title: Datadog: "Designing MCP tools for agents: lessons from building Datadog's MCP server"
findings.what: Reilly Wood, 2026-03-04. CSV uses about half the tokens per record of JSON for tabular results; YAML saves about 20% on nested data. With trimmed default fields, some tools fit about 5x more records in the same budget. Pagination is cut by a token budget, not by a record count, and returns a cursor. Letting the agent write SQL (GROUP BY, LIMIT) instead of fetching raw logs made some evaluation scenarios about 40% cheaper. Errors suggest a fix ("unknown field 'stauts' - did you mean 'status'?").
findings.lesson: The most direct template for the output of a query command: CSV for flat results, a default projection with fewer columns, a limit expressed in tokens with an explicit way to get more, aggregation pushed into SQL, and errors that name the nearest valid field. The effect of the error messages is asserted, not measured.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Numbers are Datadog's own, evaluation setup not described.

findings.title: Axiom: "Designing MCP servers for wide events"
findings.what: Neil Jagdish Patel, 2025-10-07. For 5 rows x 6 fields, CSV is 166 tokens versus 235 for minified JSON (-29%, o200k_base). The server applies a global budget of cells per result (totals and summaries first, then data tables), keeps the top N columns of wide schemas by a score (fill rate, cardinality, common names), caps at the source (an uncapped query could return 50,000 groups), defaults to a narrow time window, and writes explicit truncation notes ("Showing 100 of 2,340 rows").
findings.lesson: "Start small, expand on demand": bound results inside the query rather than in the formatter, say exactly what was cut and how to get the rest, and give summary statistics priority over raw rows. The stated cost: CSV loses types and nesting, so types must come from the schema description.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Token counts are small worked examples, no task accuracy measured.

findings.title: Format benchmarks: Improving Agents (table formats, TOON) versus the TOON repository's own benchmark
findings.what: Improving Agents (2025-09-30 and 2025-10-28): 1,000 lookup questions over 1,000 flat records, GPT-4.1-nano. Markdown key-value 60.7% (52k tokens), XML 56.0%, YAML 54.7%, JSON 52.3% (66k), Markdown table 51.9% (25k), TOON 47.5% (21.5k), CSV 44.3% (19.5k); 95% intervals about +/-3 points. On nested data (GPT-5-nano) YAML 62.1%, TOON 43.1% (last). The TOON repo (https://github.com/toon-format/toon; 244 questions, 4 models) reports TOON 72.2% versus JSON 71.4% with 42.6% fewer tokens, and on flat data TOON 63.1% versus CSV 62.2% with CSV about 6% smaller.
findings.lesson: Token savings of compact formats are consistent across sources; accuracy rankings are not. In the TOON repo the differences between formats are smaller than the stated +/-2.8 to 4.6 margins, so they do not show any format to be better. The Improving Agents test puts 1,000 rows in context without repeated headers, which is the situation a data layer should avoid anyway. Practical reading: use CSV or a Markdown table for small flat results, keep results small, and do not adopt TOON for tabular data.
findings.verified: Both Improving Agents pages and the TOON README read. Single small models in the independent tests; the authors list this caveat. A third-party summary (dev.to) was read but not relied on.

findings.title: Anthropic: "Writing effective tools for agents - with agents"
findings.what: 2025-09-11. Recommendations: a response_format parameter (concise 72 tokens versus detailed 206 in the Slack example), a combination of pagination, filtering and truncation with sensible defaults (Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens), truncation messages that steer toward narrower queries, errors that are specific and actionable, semantic names instead of UUIDs, namespaced tool names. No output format (XML, JSON, Markdown) is best in general. Method: build realistic multi-step tasks with verifiable answers, measure accuracy, calls, tokens and tool errors, keep a held-out test set.
findings.lesson: The transferable part is the method: write 20 to 50 realistic questions with known answers against your own interface, read the transcripts, and change descriptions and outputs based on where the agent wastes calls. Most specific recommendations in the post come with examples, not numbers.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Held-out accuracy gains are shown only in charts, no figures in the text.

findings.title: Cursor: "Dynamic context discovery"
findings.what: Jediah Katz, 2026-01-06. Five uses of files as the interface: long tool outputs are written to a file that the agent reads with tail/grep instead of being truncated; chat history kept as a file after summarisation; skills (name + description in the prompt, body on demand); MCP tool descriptions synced to folders with only names in the prompt; terminal sessions as files. The MCP-as-files change cut total agent tokens by 46.9% in an A/B test on runs that called an MCP tool.
findings.lesson: Large outputs should go to a file and the agent should receive a path plus a short preview. Truncation loses data; a file keeps it retrievable. This is the pattern behind a 'pull' command. The 46.9% is the only measured figure (reported as statistically significant, sample size and baseline not given).
findings.verified: Read on the primary page.

findings.title: Mintlify ChromaFs: a virtual read-only file system over an existing index, instead of a sandbox per session
findings.what: 2026-03-24. The docs assistant gets ls/cd/find/cat/grep through just-bash (Vercel Labs, bash reimplemented in TypeScript with a pluggable file system) backed by the Chroma index that already existed. The file tree is a gzipped JSON document, cat joins chunks, grep is a coarse filter in Chroma then an in-memory grep. P90 session start about 46 s (sandbox) --> about 100 ms; marginal cost about $0.0137 per conversation --> about 0; 30,000+ conversations per day. Writes raise EROFS; the tree is pruned by the user's permissions.
findings.lesson: The 'file system' can be a facade: agents need the shell vocabulary, not real files or a real container. A read-only facade is stateless and enforces access control by what is visible. The post measures infrastructure only (start time, cost), not answer quality.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. No evaluation of accuracy against the previous RAG approach.

findings.title: Block: "Block's playbook for designing MCP servers"
findings.what: Salman Mohammed and Kalvin Chau, 2025-06-16, from more than 60 internal MCP servers. Design from workflows, not from endpoints. The Google Calendar server v2 syncs events into DuckDB tables and exposes one query_database tool plus macros (free_slots). The Linear server went from 30+ tools to 2 (read-only query, mutation query) with the schema in the instructions. Check output size before returning; reject with an actionable message (Goose refuses files over 400 KB and suggests sed -n). Keep prompts stable for caching (no timestamps). Separate read tools from write tools.
findings.lesson: Independent convergence on 'sync into DuckDB, expose one query tool, put the schema in the instructions, add macros for recurring questions'. Macros or saved views for frequent questions are a cheap addition to a query interface.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Examples are qualitative (calls reduced from 4-6 to 1), no accuracy figures.

findings.title: Justin Poehnelt: "You need to rewrite your CLI for AI agents" (Google Workspace CLI, gws)
findings.what: 2026-03-04, about the open-source gws CLI. Recommendations: raw JSON payload input instead of many flags, a 'schema <method>' command that returns parameters and types at runtime, field masks to limit response size, JSON or NDJSON output when stdout is not a terminal, --page-all with one JSON object per page, --dry-run, input hardening (reject control characters, confine output paths), 100+ SKILL.md files, and the same commands exposed over MCP.
findings.lesson: An agent-friendly CLI is self-describing at runtime (the agent asks the CLI for the schema, the skill file stays short), lets the caller select fields, and treats agent input as untrusted. This matches a list | describe | query | pull design closely. Evidence: none measured; it is a practitioner's design rationale.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page. Author's affiliation not stated on the page.

findings.title: Sandboxes for code over data: LangChain "The two patterns by which agents connect sandboxes" (plus Pydantic Monty, Turso AgentFS)
findings.what: Harrison Chase, 2026-02-10: either the agent runs inside the sandbox (direct file access, but API keys sit inside it and the agent has no more privileges than its bash tool) or the sandbox is a remote tool (keys stay outside, pay per execution, latency per call); providers named: E2B, Modal, Daytona, Runloop. Pydantic Monty (https://github.com/pydantic/monty) is a Python-subset interpreter in Rust with no file system or network unless passed in, start under 1 ms versus about 1,500 ms for a sandbox service. Turso AgentFS (https://turso.tech/blog/agentfs, 2025-11-13) stores an agent's files, key-value state and an append-only log of tool calls in one SQLite file, mountable with FUSE.
findings.lesson: Three levels exist: full container or VM, an in-process restricted interpreter, and a virtual file system. For a data layer consumed by coding agents that already have a shell, the sandbox is the client's problem; the server only needs a read-only query path. An audit log of calls that is itself queryable is a cheap feature worth copying.
findings.verified: All three primary pages read. No performance or accuracy comparisons between providers; AgentFS describes its sandbox part as highly experimental. E2B, Modal and Daytona documentation not read. DuckDB-WASM and Pyodide as agent sandboxes not checked (search budget exhausted).

findings.title: llms.txt and Markdown endpoints: llmstxt.org and Cloudflare "Markdown for Agents"
findings.what: llms.txt (Jeremy Howard, 2024-09-03, https://llmstxt.org/): a Markdown index at the site root with an H1, a summary and lists of links, plus a .md version of each page; intended for use at inference time. Cloudflare (2026-02-12) converts HTML to Markdown at the edge when a client sends Accept: text/markdown, and returns an x-markdown-tokens header; its own post is 16,180 tokens as HTML and 3,150 as Markdown (about -80%). It states that Claude Code and OpenCode already send that header. The MCP documentation itself points agents to its llms.txt index.
findings.lesson: Serving Markdown and a short index is cheap and coding agents do request it. The evidence covers token size and what publishers do; nothing I read measures whether agents complete tasks better with llms.txt. For a small data layer, the equivalent is a compact 'list' output and a Markdown 'describe' with a token count.
findings.verified: Both primary pages read. Adoption claims are from the authors themselves. No independent study of whether models actually fetch llms.txt was found (search budget exhausted before I could look).

patterns: Progressive disclosure: put only names and one-line descriptions in the prompt and let the agent load details on demand; measured token savings of 47% to 85% (Cursor A/B test, Anthropic tool search), same design in Agent Skills, Anthropic code execution with MCP, Cloudflare Code Mode.

Files are used for context and documentation, SQL for the data: Vercel d0 keeps the semantic layer as YAML/Markdown files and still executes SQL; the Vercel + Braintrust test shows SQL at 100% and about 7x fewer tokens than bash over JSON files; Block and Datadog both moved to a single query tool.
Fewer, more general tools replace one tool per endpoint: Vercel d0 (17 --> 2), Block Linear (30+ --> 2), Cloudflare (2,500 endpoints --> search + execute), Datadog (small default toolset).

Results are bounded by a token or cell budget, with an explicit note on what was cut and how to get more; large outputs go to a file with a path returned: Anthropic writing tools (25,000-token cap), Datadog (pagination by tokens), Axiom (cell budget, 'Showing 100 of 2,340 rows'), Cursor (outputs to files), Manus (restorable compression), Block (400 KB refusal with a hint).
