Compact tabular output: CSV saves about 30% to 50% of tokens versus JSON for flat rows (Datadog, Axiom, TOON repo), but accuracy rankings of formats contradict each other and differences are often within the margin of error (Improving Agents, TOON repo, Anthropic: 'no single format is best').

Errors are written as instructions for the next call (nearest valid field, expected format, narrower query), and failed calls are kept in context: Datadog, Anthropic writing tools, Block, Manus. All by example; none of these sources measures the effect.

A virtual or read-only file system facade is replacing per-session containers where the agent only reads: Mintlify ChromaFs on just-bash (46 s --> 100 ms), Pydantic Monty (under 1 ms), Turso AgentFS; LangChain describes the full-container alternatives (E2B, Modal, Daytona, Runloop).

Evaluation on your own tasks is the recommended arbiter, and public numbers are thin: Anthropic's method (realistic tasks, held-out set, read transcripts), the Vercel + Braintrust post finding 5 wrong reference answers, Vercel d0 resting on 5 queries, LlamaIndex on 5 questions.
disagreements: Bash and files versus SQL. Vercel d0 (2025-12) presents 'bash is all you need'; one month later Vercel + Braintrust measure bash over JSON files at 52.7% versus SQL at 100% on structured data. The two are compatible only if files hold the documentation and SQL holds the data.

File tools versus vector search. LlamaIndex (2026-01-13, https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/did-filesystem-tools-kill-vector-search): on 5 papers the file agent scores higher (correctness 8.4 versus 6.4 out of 10) but is slower (11.2 s versus 7.4 s); at 100 to 1,000 documents RAG is faster and slightly more correct. Five questions per condition, so this is an indication only. Mintlify and LangChain argue for files without measuring answer quality.

Does TOON (or any format) improve accuracy? The TOON repo says slightly yes versus JSON (72.2% versus 71.4%, inside the +/-2.8 margin, so not a demonstrated difference); Improving Agents finds TOON 9th of 12 on flat data and last on nested data, and CSV near the bottom on a 1,000-row lookup, while the TOON repo has CSV level with TOON on flat data. Models, table sizes and question types differ, so no general ranking holds.

Code execution versus direct tool calls. Anthropic, Cloudflare and the CodeAct paper (arXiv 2402.01030, up to 20% higher success over 17 models) favour code; Anthropic's own measured accuracy gain from programmatic calling is small (25.6% --> 28.5%), and all sources note the added cost of running a sandbox.

Dynamic tool loading versus a stable prompt. Anthropic tool search and Cursor load definitions on demand; Manus argues against adding or removing tools during a task because it invalidates the prompt cache and confuses the model, and prefers masking.

MCP resources versus tools. The MCP specification defines resources as application-driven (the host decides what enters context) and tools as model-controlled. Every production write-up read here exposes data and schema through tools or files, not resources; I found no evidence that agents use resources well. This is an absence of evidence in my sample, not a measured result.

Limits of this search: the web search budget of the session ran out after 6 queries, so the remaining sources were fetched from known URLs. Not checked: independent studies of llms.txt uptake, E2B/Modal/Daytona documentation, DuckDB-WASM or Pyodide as agent sandboxes, any measured effect of error messages with recovery hints, papers on schema pagination.
results.for_adele: The evidence supports the current shape: SQL through DuckDB for data, files and a CLI for discovery. Keep `list` tiny (name + one line), make `describe` the on-demand detail (fields, units, grain, coverage, 3 sample rows, one or two example queries: examples had the largest measured effect). `query` should default to CSV or a Markdown table, apply a row or token cap in the query itself, and print "showing N of M, use pull or narrow the filter". `pull` returns a path, not rows. Errors should name the nearest valid column or dataset. Skip MCP resources and TOON. Keep SKILL.md short and let the CLI describe itself. Add a log of calls and 20 to 30 questions with known answers to test changes.

findings.title: Supporting Our AI Overlords: Redesigning Data Systems to be Agent-First (UC Berkeley, CIDR 2026)
findings.what: Vision paper (Liu, Ponnapalli, Shankar, Zeighami, Zhu, ..., Stoica, Zaharia, Parameswaran). It names the workload of agents 'agentic speculation' and gives it four traits: scale, heterogeneity (metadata exploration, column statistics, partial queries, full queries), redundancy, steerability. Case study 1 (BIRD on DuckDB, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B): success rises by 14 to 70% with more attempts, and across 50 attempts the distinct sub-plans are often under 10 to 20% of the total. Case study 2 (o3 agent, 44 traces): grounding hints cut SQL queries per trace from 12.67 to 10.38 (-18%), and partial query attempts by 37%. Proposals: 'probes' (SQL plus a natural-language brief stating goal, phase and accuracy need), 'sleeper agents' in the database that return related tables, why-not explanations for empty results and cost estimates, a persistent 'agentic memory store' of earlier probes and learned metadata (encodings, missing-value markers, grain), approximate answers during exploration, cheap branching.
findings.lesson: Expect an agent to send many small, overlapping exploration queries before one real query. Make that phase cheap and informative: answer metadata and statistics questions without a table scan, return hints with every answer (join candidates, why a result is empty, estimated cost), and keep what earlier sessions learned about a dataset in a place where the next session can read it.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv HTML v2 through WebFetch (numbers above come from it) and the CIDR 2026 proceedings index. The summary noted that the text says 'more than 20%' fewer queries while Table 1 shows 14 to 37%. The Neon figure (agents create 20x more branches and 50x more rollbacks than humans) is quoted by the paper, not checked at Neon.

findings.title: DAB: Data Agent Benchmark (UC Berkeley EPIC lab with Hasura PromptQL)
findings.what: Benchmark built after a formative study of six enterprises. Paper HTML: 104 queries, 17 datasets, 4 engines (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, SQLite, DuckDB); 73% of queries need reconciliation of badly formatted join keys, 84% need values extracted from free text, 62% need domain knowledge. Best pass@1 is 57% (GPT-5.5 in Codex), 52% (Gemini 3.1 Pro), 48% (Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Claude Code); no agent exceeds 70% pass@5. Of the wrong answers, 57% are incorrect implementation, 31% incorrect plan, only 11% incorrect data selection, 1% no attempt. Removing hints changes accuracy by -0.04 to +0.02; removing hints and descriptions costs 0.02 to 0.05 and raises exploratory calls (Gemini: 23.6% --> 40.9% of calls).
findings.lesson: Agents usually find the right table and column. They fail later, silently, in the plan and the code: a regex for a year that matches inside an ISBN, 'MALE' matching inside 'FEMALE', an average of averages, an unrequested LIMIT. So the data layer should remove the need for ad hoc parsing (typed dates, clean join keys, categorical codes, canonical units done once at ingestion) and should state grain and aggregation rules, because the schema description alone does not prevent these errors. Descriptions mainly save exploration cost.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv HTML (both halves) and the GitHub README (github.com/ucbepic/DataAgentBench). The two disagree: the README states 54 queries and 12 datasets and shows a leaderboard with pass@1 of 0.99 for a system that uses a semantic layer, hints and a tuned prompt; the paper states 104 queries and 17 datasets with 57% best. I did not resolve this (the 54-query set matches the paper's 'shared harness' subset). The failure labels come from an LLM judge; a human matched it exactly on 67% of 30 trajectories.

findings.title: KramaBench: data-to-insight pipelines over data lakes (MIT, Kraska/Madden/Cafarella groups)
findings.what: 104 hand-solved tasks over 1,700 files from 24 sources in 6 domains; the agent must discover files, clean, integrate and compute. Best system reaches 55.8% end to end (smolagents deep research with Claude 3.7); with the gold files given it reaches only about 61 to 63%; human baseline 76.75%. Agents identify up to 42% of the key pipeline steps and fully implement about 22% of sub-tasks. Named failures: an 'M' code for missing values not recognised, a 'Beach Name' column that encodes two things, near-duplicate files and undocumented schemas. A failure diagnosis attributes 24% (o3) and 43% (Claude) of failed tasks to not asking for clarification.
findings.lesson: Retrieval of the right file is the smaller problem (0 to 7% gain from oracle files). The larger one is undocumented conventions inside the data: sentinel codes for missing values, columns with two meanings, near-duplicate tables. Document or normalise these per column, and give each dataset one canonical table instead of several look-alike files.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page and the first 100,000 characters of the HTML v3. The source has an internal inconsistency on the 'obscured input' result (12.77% in text, 13.94% in table).

findings.title: DS-STAR (Google Cloud and KAIST) on DABStep, KramaBench, DA-Code
findings.what: Multi-agent system for data science with a 'data file analyzer' (writes a script that summarises the structure and content of every file before planning), an LLM verifier that judges whether the plan is sufficient, and a router that backtracks. On DABStep hard tasks: 45.24% full system, 39.95% without router, 34.66% without verifier, 26.98% without the file analyzer (Gemini 2.5 Pro alone: 12.70%). KramaBench 39.8% --> 44.7%, DA-Code 37.0% --> 38.5%. Cost: about 3.5x the input tokens of ReAct.
findings.lesson: The component whose removal costs the most is the one that describes the data files up front (18 points on hard tasks). This is direct ablation evidence that a precomputed 'describe' output (structure, types, sample rows, value ranges) is the highest-value thing a data layer can hand an agent, and that 'the code ran' is not evidence of a correct answer.
findings.verified: Read the first 100,000 characters of arXiv HTML v4 through WebFetch; ablation table taken from there. One benchmark (DABStep), one base model: the size of the effect may not transfer.

findings.title: DABStep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (Adyen and Hugging Face)
findings.what: 450 tasks derived from real work at a payments company: one 138,000-row CSV, a column readme, fee rules in JSON, and a manual.md with domain definitions. 72 easy tasks (best 80.56%) and 378 hard tasks (best 14.55% at publication, o4-mini). Failure analysis: agents consult the documentation too late or not at all, skip intermediate computations (for example they filter on a monthly fraud rate without computing it), ignore output format rules, and some reasoning models score near 0% with the standard ReAct prompt.
findings.lesson: Even with one clean table, the hard part is business rules that are written in prose. Having a manual is not enough: agents read it late. Put definitions and computation rules where the agent cannot miss them (in the describe output, next to the field) and, where a derived quantity is standard, precompute it as a column or view.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page and HTML. The 'recommendations' in the fetched summary are partly inferred from the failure analysis, not stated by the authors. Hard tasks are permutations of 23 core questions, so the 378 tasks are not 378 independent observations.

findings.title: Ambig-DS: task-framing ambiguity in data-science agents
findings.what: Two diagnostic suites (51 tasks from DSBench, 61 from MLE-bench) where each task has a fully specified and an ambiguous variant; 5 agents. Under ambiguity the dominant failure is a 'silent commitment': the agent picks one plausible reading (wrong target, wrong metric) and delivers clean, runnable output. One clarifying question recovers much of the loss, but agents do not know when to ask: a permissive prompt makes them ask on clear tasks, a conservative prompt makes them default silently.
findings.lesson: Silent wrong answers come from ambiguity at least as much as from bad SQL. A data layer cannot make the agent ask, but it can remove ambiguity on its side: one name per concept, explicit units and time zone, explicit grain, and a SKILL.md rule that tells the agent to state the interpretation it chose (which column, which unit, which period) in its answer.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page only. Percentages of unflagged misframing (39 to 63%) come from a secondary summary in search results, not from the paper.

findings.title: Text-to-SQL Benchmarks are Broken: annotation errors in BIRD and Spider 2.0-Snow (Jin, Choi, Zhu, Kang; CIDR 2026)
findings.what: Expert audit finds annotation errors in 52.8% of BIRD Mini-Dev and 62.8% of Spider 2.0-Snow examples. After correcting a BIRD Dev subset and re-running 16 open-source agents, relative performance changes by -7% to +31% and ranks move by up to 9 positions; rank correlation with the original leaderboard falls from 0.85 to 0.32.
findings.lesson: Leaderboard differences of a few points on these benchmarks are not evidence for a design choice. For Adele, a small set of hand-verified questions on your own datasets (with the expected number, unit and period) is more trustworthy than any public score, and the questions themselves must be reviewed for ambiguity.
findings.verified: Read the arXiv abstract page (v3); title on arXiv is 'Pervasive Annotation Errors Break Text-to-SQL Benchmarks and Leaderboards', CIDR title confirmed on the proceedings index. Related context read on spider2-sql.github.io: the Snow leaderboard now shows 96.7 at the top while Spider 2.0-DBT tops at 65.6, which fits the saturation and reliability concern but is my reading, not the paper's.

findings.title: BridgeScope: a toolkit between LLM agents and databases (Alibaba, CIDR 2026)
findings.what: Open-source toolkit for PostgreSQL exposed as MCP tools. Three ideas: split SQL access into fine-grained tools (context retrieval, CRUD, transactions); make the tool list reflect the privileges of the user, so the agent sees early that a task is infeasible; a proxy that moves result data from one tool to the next without passing it through the model. Reported: 23 to 71% fewer reasoning steps and 30 to 82% lower token cost, 'up to 80%' in the abstract.
findings.lesson: Two design rules transfer directly: (1) large results should go to a file or to the next tool, not through the context of the model (Adele's 'pull' to local Parquet is the same idea); (2) the interface should show the agent what it cannot do before it tries, instead of failing after several steps.
findings.verified: Read the abstract, introduction and the numeric lines of the PDF text (extracted locally with pdftotext). I did not read the evaluation section in full; the two benchmarks are the authors' own.

findings.title: Please Don't Kill My Vibe: Empowering Agents with Data Flow Control (Columbia, CIDR 2026)
findings.what: Position paper with an early prototype. It argues that policy violations, corrupted state and prompt injection in agent work on databases are all undesirable data flows, and that the DBMS should enforce 'data flow control' policies natively, using provenance of each output row, the same way validation and access control once moved from applications into the database. Model-centric safety and human approval of every action are judged insufficient.
findings.lesson: Enforce constraints in the data system, not in the prompt. For a read-only layer the equivalent is small: a read-only connection, row and time limits enforced by the CLI, and text fields from external sources treated as untrusted data (a dataset description fetched from the web can carry injected instructions).
findings.verified: Read the abstract and introduction of the PDF text (extracted locally). No quantitative evaluation was seen in the parts read. The application to a read-only layer is my inference.

findings.title: BEAVER (enterprise text-to-SQL) and 'Beyond the Harness' (context artifacts from query history)
findings.what: BEAVER (arXiv 2409.02038) is built from private data warehouses and real query logs; in the v2 paper GPT-4o reaches 0% with retrieved tables, 2.1% with gold tables, 4.2% with gold tables plus column mappings; error analysis of 50 questions: wrong column mapping 59.1%, missed implicit assumptions 50.0%. 'Beyond the Harness' (Gwimm and Eisenach, workshop paper, Aug 2026) distils historical production SQL into 'SQL reference cards' and table cards: on 5,176 internal queries of a large retailer, improving the context artifacts gives about 12 to 25% gain in AST similarity versus about 3 to 12% for improving the retrieval harness. On BEAVER the best variant scores 9.00% versus 6.33% baseline, p = 0.12 on 300 held-out queries.
findings.lesson: Example queries that are known to be correct are a context artifact in their own right, and the content of the context matters more than the retrieval machinery around it. A few validated SQL examples per dataset in the descriptor are cheap to add. Caveat: the public-benchmark result is not established. p = 0.12 means that a difference this large would appear in about 12% of repeated samples even if the method had no effect, so the BEAVER gain could be chance; the internal result uses AST similarity, which measures resemblance to the reference SQL, not correctness of the answer.
findings.verified: Read both arXiv pages (abstract page for 2608.22830, HTML v2 for BEAVER). The 42 to 44% share of schema-linking errors and the 10.8% figure for a newer model come from search snippets only.

findings.title: LiveSQLBench and BIRD-Interact (HKU BIRD team with Google Cloud)
findings.what: LiveSQLBench is a continuously refreshed benchmark built from updated CSV datasets, with SELECT and data-management tasks, each database paired with a 'hierarchical knowledge base' of linked business definitions (JSON now, documents planned). Large-v1 (March 2026): 18 databases with about 1,000 columns each, about 84,000 prompt tokens on average. Top leaderboard entry 57.0%; best plain model listed 35.5%. Agent evaluation costs about 15x direct generation ($0.89 versus $0.06 per task for one model). BIRD-Interact (arXiv 2510.05318, ICLR 2026 oral) adds a simulated user and ambiguity: GPT-5 completes 8.67% in the scripted protocol and 17.00% in the agentic mode.
findings.lesson: The benchmark community now treats a knowledge base of definitions as part of the database, next to the schema, and tests whether the agent applies a chain of linked definitions. This supports shipping definitions (derived metrics, business terms) in a structured, linkable form inside the descriptor, not in free prose elsewhere.
findings.verified: Read the LiveSQLBench site and the BIRD-Interact arXiv abstract page. The site does not label every leaderboard entry's category, so the 57.0% versus 35.5% comparison is approximate.

findings.title: Automatic Metadata Extraction for Text-to-SQL (AT&T: Shkapenyuk, Srivastava, Johnson, Ghane)
findings.what: Studies metadata that can be produced without domain experts: database profiling, analysis of query logs, and LLM-generated text descriptions of SQL. With profiling alone and GPT-4o (no fine-tuned model) the system held first place on the BIRD leaderboard in several periods of 2024 and again from March to at least May 2025, with and without the benchmark's 'oracle' hints.
findings.lesson: Machine-generated profiles per column (null share, distinct count, min and max, typical formats, frequent values) are effective metadata and cost nothing to maintain, because DuckDB can regenerate them at every refresh. Hand-written descriptions can then be reserved for what profiling cannot find: units, meaning, known caveats.
findings.verified: Abstract page only; the HTML version returned 404, so I have no ablation numbers and the list of profile fields in the lesson is my expectation of what 'profiling' contains, not a quote. BIRD rankings are subject to the annotation-error caveat above.

findings.title: Deep Research is the New Analytics System (Russo and Kraska, MIT, CIDR 2026)
findings.what: Argues that OLAP engines, semantic-operator systems (Palimpzest, LOTUS, DocETL) and deep-research code agents all do the same job (plan, execute, return), and that the runtime should let a code agent write programs over optimised operators. Prototype on two queries (one from KramaBench): up to 1.95x better F1 than an open deep-research agent, and 76.8% cost and 72.7% runtime savings versus an agent that calls semantic operators as plain tools.
findings.lesson: The trend in research is 'the agent writes a program against a good engine', not 'the agent calls many narrow tools'. This agrees with DAB's observation that the cheapest and most accurate agent wrote one larger program per question with a 4:1 ratio of database calls to Python calls. A CLI that accepts arbitrary SQL fits this direction.
findings.verified: Read abstract and introduction of the PDF text (extracted locally) and the numeric lines. Evidence is two queries, which is an illustration, not a measurement of a general effect.

patterns: Schema discovery is no longer the main bottleneck for frontier agents; plan and implementation errors are (DAB: 11% wrong data selection versus 88% plan or implementation; KramaBench: oracle files add only 0 to 7%; 'The Death of Schema Linking?' reaches the same position for text-to-SQL).

Failures are silent: the code runs and the answer is wrong, because of a wrong reading of the task, an undocumented convention in the data, or an ad hoc parse (Ambig-DS, DAB regex cases, KramaBench missing-value code, DS-STAR's argument that successful execution is not verification).

A description of the data handed over before planning is the context with the best measured effect, and it mostly reduces exploration cost when the model is strong (DS-STAR ablation: -18 points on hard tasks without the file analyzer; agent-first paper: -18% queries with grounding hints; DAB: exploratory calls nearly double without descriptions; AT&T profiling paper).

Domain rules and definitions are treated as a first-class artifact next to the schema, and agents use them badly when they are only prose in a manual (DABStep manual.md consulted too late, LiveSQLBench hierarchical knowledge base, BIRD-Interact, Beyond the Harness reference cards).

Agent workloads are many small, redundant, exploratory requests, so the system should make exploration cheap, answer with hints, and remember what was learned (agent-first paper: probes, sleeper agents, agentic memory store; LiveSQLBench: agent mode costs about 15x direct generation).

Safety and efficiency constraints should be enforced by the data system and reflected in the interface, not requested in the prompt (Please Don't Kill My Vibe: data flow control; BridgeScope: tools that mirror privileges and a proxy that keeps bulk data out of the model context).

Public benchmark scores for data agents are unreliable guides for design choices (CIDR 2026 annotation-error audit: 52.8% and 62.8% faulty examples and reshuffled rankings; DABStep hard set derived from 23 core questions; DAB leaderboard entries with tuned prompts and author-derived hints; Spider 2.0-Snow near 97%).

The preferred execution model is a code agent that writes a larger program against a capable engine instead of many narrow tool calls (DAB behaviour analysis, Russo and Kraska, KramaBench where iterative code agents beat fixed pipelines).
disagreements: Do descriptions and hints raise accuracy? DS-STAR finds a large gain from describing files (26.98% --> 45.24% on DABStep hard), while DAB finds that removing hints and descriptions moves pass@1 by only 0.02 to 0.05 and that a hint once led an agent to abandon a correct answer. Likely reconciliation (my reading): strong agents can rebuild a description by exploring, at a cost, so the gain shows up as fewer calls more than as accuracy; neither paper reports confidence intervals that would settle it.

Explore step by step or write one large program? The agent-first paper treats massive speculation as the workload to support (accuracy up 14 to 70% with more attempts), while DAB reports that the agent with the fewest calls and the largest programs was both cheapest and most accurate, and DS-STAR gains accuracy from more refinement rounds at 3.5x token cost.

Should the database itself contain LLM components (probe interpreter, sleeper agents, semantic operators), as the Berkeley and MIT vision papers propose, or stay a plain engine behind a thin toolkit (BridgeScope, and the practice of all the benchmarks)? The vision papers have case studies and prototypes on a handful of queries, not production evidence.

Schema pruning: older pipelines and BEAVER (89% of retrieval failures are 'insufficient information retrieved') treat table retrieval as critical; 'The Death of Schema Linking?' and DAB say that strong models cope with the full schema when it fits in context. The answer depends on schema size (BEAVER and LiveSQLBench-Large have about 1,000 columns per database), which is far from a dozen tables.

When should the agent ask instead of assume? Ambig-DS, KramaBench (24 to 43% of failures attributed to not asking) and BIRD-Interact say that asking helps, but Ambig-DS also shows that no prompt setting gets the timing right (over-asking on clear tasks or silent defaults on ambiguous ones).

How much to trust any of these numbers: the CIDR 2026 audit claims that more than half of BIRD Mini-Dev and Spider 2.0-Snow examples are faulty, which undercuts results (including the AT&T metadata paper and BEAVER comparisons) that rest on those leaderboards. The DAB repository and the DAB paper also state different sizes and very different top scores.

Coverage limit of this search: the session's web search budget ran out after five queries, so the list was completed by fetching known primary URLs. Not checked: InsightBench and DA-Code primary pages, SIGMOD/VLDB 2026 proceedings, any TPC-style proposal for agent workloads, and any study that isolates unit or time-zone errors (I found none, which is not evidence that none exists).
results.for_adele: The research supports Adele's shape (describe before query, arbitrary SQL, pull to file) and shifts the effort toward ingestion. Agents find the right table; they fail silently on parsing, grain and conventions. So: normalise at ingestion (typed timestamps with explicit time zone, canonical units, clean join keys, explicit null instead of sentinel codes), and put in each descriptor the grain, allowed aggregations, definitions of derived quantities, a machine-generated column profile, and two or three validated example queries. Make `describe` cheap and complete so exploration costs few calls. Have query results repeat units, period and row count. In SKILL.md, require the agent to state its interpretation. Evaluate with a small set of hand-verified questions on your own data, not public leaderboards.

findings.title: UK government: Guidelines and best practices for making government datasets ready for AI (GDS / DSIT / DCMS)
findings.what: Published 19 January 2026. Four pillars (technical optimisation, data and metadata quality, organisation and infrastructure, legal/security/ethics), a yes/no self-assessment checklist of 24 items, and a readiness score on a 4-point scale. Concrete demands: Parquet or Iceberg instead of CSV for anything large; keep several grains and document which use each grain supports (aggregated 'gold' tables are called unsuitable for training); OpenAPI REST with pagination and rate limits; MCP servers named explicitly for agentic access; versioned schemas with a deprecation policy; published ownership, licence, update schedule and quality status; DCAT and Dublin Core metadata; documented purpose of collection, decision rules and known biases. Croissant and schema.org are not named.
findings.lesson: The most concrete official checklist found. The 'metadata fitness' block is directly reusable as a descriptor test: every field defined, event time and update frequency and history clear, schema versions tracked, provenance known, quality issues documented, stable IDs present or their absence stated explicitly.
findings.verified: Read the HTML version of the guidance through WebFetch (model summary of the page, not the 44-page PDF). The item counts per checklist block come from that summary.

findings.title: World Bank Data360 MCP server (AI for Data team)
findings.what: MCP server over the Data360 indicator platform, built with Python 3.11+ and FastMCP, PyPI version 0.1.3, 45 stars, 394 commits. Six tools: search indicators (with a server-side check of country coverage), get data, get metadata with a `select_fields` parameter, get disaggregation (the available filter values), find codelist value (Kenya --> KEN), list indicators. Six resources including `data360://system-prompt` and `data360://codelists`. The README states the goal as answering 'without hallucinating data values' and describes the layer as glue that makes the raw API 'composable and safe for LLM tool use'.
findings.lesson: A publisher-built layer converges on the same verbs as Adele (search, describe, query) plus two that Adele lacks: a resolver from names to codes, and a call that lists the valid filter values of a dimension before the query is written. Metadata is fetched on demand and field by field, to keep the agent's context small.
findings.verified: Read the GitHub README through WebFetch. 'Official' is inferred from the worldbank organisation and the team contact; the README does not use the word. No release date visible.

findings.title: Data Commons MCP server and agent toolkit (Google)
findings.what: Announced 24 September 2025 (Google Developers Blog), docs last updated 9 November 2026. Hosted endpoint https://api.datacommons.org/mcp with a free API key; also the PyPI package `datacommons-mcp` in the repo datacommonsorg/agent-toolkit (Apache-2.0, 149 stars). Six tools: `search_indicators`, `search_child_indicators`, `get_variable_metadata`, `get_observations`, `get_child_observations`, `get_multi_entity_observations`. The server now ships 'skills' as MCP resources: playbooks for three workflows (one place, child places, pairs of places with a direction such as exports). Stated limits: no events, no graph exploration, no output for visualisation.
findings.lesson: Even the largest public statistics graph exposes only a few intent-shaped tools (search, metadata, observations) and then adds written playbooks, served by the server itself, so that the client needs no dataset-specific prompt. This is the same pairing as Adele's CLI plus SKILL.md, with the skill travelling with the data layer.
findings.verified: Read docs.datacommons.org/mcp, the run_tools page, the Google Developers Blog post and the repo page through WebFetch. The ONE Data Agent example ('tens of millions' of health financing data points) comes from the blog post only.

findings.title: datagouv-mcp: official MCP server of data.gouv.fr
findings.what: Described in its README as the official data.gouv.fr MCP server. MIT, 1.6k stars, 270 commits, Python with uv and the official MCP SDK, Streamable HTTP only. Public endpoint https://mcp.data.gouv.fr/mcp, no key, read-only. Ten tools: search datasets and organisations, dataset info, list resources, resource info (which says whether the Tabular API can serve the file), `query_resource_data` (rows through the Tabular API, default page 20, maximum 200; CSV up to 100 MB, XLSX up to 12.5 MB), three tools for third-party APIs including one that returns a summary of an OpenAPI spec, and usage metrics.
findings.lesson: A national portal with tens of thousands of heterogeneous files cannot offer SQL over everything. It offers a fixed path (search --> list resources --> check that the file is queryable --> paginated rows) and falls back to the raw file URL for large files. Adele's `pull` plays the role of that fallback. The explicit 'is this resource queryable' flag is worth copying.
findings.verified: Read the repo page and README through WebFetch. No release dates on the page. Did not test the endpoint.

findings.title: U.S. Census Bureau Data API MCP server
findings.what: Repo under the uscensusbureau organisation, CC0, TypeScript on the MCP SDK, 107 stars, 152 commits. Four tools: `list-datasets`, `fetch-dataset-geography`, `fetch-aggregate-data`, `resolve-geography-fips`; one prompt (`get_population_data`). The server runs locally with Docker Compose and seeds a local PostgreSQL database with Census metadata, 'to support faster search'. A Census API key is required.
findings.lesson: The hard part of public statistics for an agent is the mapping of names to identifiers (place names to FIPS codes, variable codes), not the fetch. The Census Bureau solved it with a local, pre-seeded metadata store and a resolver tool. A small layer should index its codes and labels locally and let the agent search them.
findings.verified: Read the repo page through WebFetch. The page gives no dates and no status label (experimental or stable), so the maturity is unknown.

findings.title: Wikidata MCP (Wikimedia Deutschland)
findings.what: Released October 2025, hosted at https://wd-mcp.wmcloud.org/mcp/, code in wmde/WikidataMCP (BSD-3, 35 stars, Python with uv). Six tools: `search_items` and `search_properties` (keyword plus vector search, with a fallback to keyword only), `get_statements` (direct statements as text triples, without qualifiers or references), `get_statement_values` (full detail for one entity and property), a hierarchy tool for instance-of and subclass-of, and `execute_sparql` (CSV output, 10 rows by default). The page recommends confirming entities and properties with the other tools before writing SPARQL.
findings.lesson: Two levels of detail per entity (a short text form by default, the full form on request) and a small default row limit on the free query tool. The search tools exist so that the agent never has to guess an identifier before it writes a query.
findings.verified: Read the Wikidata project page and the GitHub README through WebFetch. The README does not explain why text triples were chosen; 'optimised for language models' is said of the separate Textifier service.

findings.title: Hugging Face Hub: automatic Parquet, dataset viewer API, `hf datasets sql`, MCP server with `hf_fs`
findings.what: Every dataset on the Hub is converted automatically to Parquet (branch `refs/convert/parquet`, written `@~parquet`) and a REST API precomputes splits, column types, size, rows, search, filter and statistics. DuckDB reads `hf://datasets/...` paths natively, and the `hf` CLI has `hf datasets sql "FROM 'hf://datasets/...' LIMIT 3"` with `--format json` for machine-readable output. The Hub's MCP server now says that most tasks are done with a single built-in tool `hf_fs`, which lets the assistant navigate the Hub like a file system.
findings.lesson: The largest dataset host ended at the same shape as Adele: Parquet behind a stable path scheme, DuckDB SQL through a CLI, JSON output for agents, precomputed statistics and first rows. Its MCP server moved towards one generic tool that navigates paths instead of many narrow tools.
findings.verified: Read the three Hugging Face docs pages (DuckDB, dataset viewer index, MCP server) directly; the text was returned verbatim. The dataset viewer page says '100,000+ datasets', which is probably an old figure.

findings.title: Our World in Data: one URL scheme per chart, with data, metadata and README
findings.what: For every chart: `/grapher/{slug}.csv`, `.metadata.json`, `.zip` (CSV + metadata + README), `.readme.md`, `.config.json`. Options `csvType=filtered`, `useColumnShortNames=true`. The metadata gives per column: short and long title, short description, key description, description of the processing, unit, short unit, timespan, last update, next update, short and long citation. Three more APIs exist (tables, semantic search of indicators, site search through Algolia), wrapped by the Python library owid-catalog. Internally, OWID documents a workflow with Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, `.claude/commands`, `.claude/agents`) for updating datasets.
findings.lesson: No MCP server is documented; the agent-ready pattern is a predictable URL per dataset that returns the data together with a metadata file and a readable README. The column metadata (a description of the processing, the date of the next update, a ready citation) is richer than a bare Frictionless field and worth adding to Adele's descriptors.
findings.verified: Read the chart API, API index, search API and AI workflow pages through WebFetch. I found no official OWID MCP page in the docs navigation; an MCP server may exist elsewhere and I could not search for it.

findings.title: ESIP checklist to examine the AI-readiness of open environmental datasets (v1.0)
findings.what: Community checklist of the ESIP Data Readiness Cluster (chair with a NOAA address), version 1.0, last updated 2023-12-20, with a fillable sheet per dataset. Four sections: preparation (gaps, outliers, gridding, whether the original sampling is still available), quality (update frequency, preliminary versus final versions, completeness in space and time, consistency of units and names over time, known bias, checksums), documentation (machine-readable data dictionary, parameters mapped to a vocabulary, DOI, contact, example code, licence, intended and non-recommended uses), access (open format, API, documentation, cloud availability).
findings.lesson: The checklist is older than agents and was written for model training, but its questions are the ones an agent needs answered per dataset: is this value preliminary, are units stable over time, what are the known gaps, what is this not suitable for. These fit as optional descriptor fields.
findings.verified: Read the README and the checklist file through WebFetch. Use by NOAA and NASA is from my memory and is not stated on the pages read.

findings.title: Croissant 1.1 (MLCommons)
findings.what: Version 1.0 dated 2024-03-01, version 1.1 dated 2026-01-29 (editors from Google and from King's College London / ODI). JSON-LD on schema.org with resources (FileObject, FileSet), structure (RecordSet, Field, keys, joins through `references`) and semantic types. Required dataset properties: name, description, license, url, creator, datePublished, distribution, conformsTo. Version 1.1 describes provenance with W3C PROV-O down to field level, usage policies (DUO, ODRL), external vocabularies, and annotations such as statistics on fields. The spec mentions agents only for discovery ('RAG over an index of Croissant descriptions').
findings.lesson: Croissant is the format that the AI-ready guidelines of the US and of ODI point to, and it overlaps strongly with a Frictionless descriptor (resources, fields, keys). It is designed for ML loaders and discovery, not for an agent that writes SQL: it has no native place for grain, freshness or sample rows. A generated Croissant export from the Frictionless descriptor would be cheap; switching formats would bring little.
findings.verified: Read both spec pages through WebFetch (first 100,000 characters of 1.1). The page has no changelog, so which features are new in 1.1 is not confirmed. Support by Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML is from memory (the HF viewer exposes a croissant endpoint).

findings.title: ODI: A framework for AI-ready data (v2, December 2025)
findings.what: The Open Data Institute published a framework that defines AI readiness with specific criteria for publishers across three areas: the data, the metadata, and the design of the infrastructure. Version 2 was added in December 2025; it is based on a literature review, expert interviews and ODI practice.
findings.lesson: The split into data, metadata and infrastructure is the same three-part split as Adele (Parquet, descriptor, CLI). The detailed criteria need to be read in the PDF before any of them is cited.
findings.verified: Landing page only. The PDF with the criteria could not be fetched (my guessed URL returned 404). Details that I remember (machine-readable metadata such as Croissant, documented provenance and licence, API and bulk access) are unverified.

findings.title: US Department of Commerce: Generative AI and Open Data, guidelines and best practices (v1.0, January 2025)
findings.what: From memory only: version 1.0 published in January 2025 by a working group of the Commerce Data Governance Board. It groups recommendations under documentation, data formats, storage and dissemination, licensing and usage, and integrity and quality. It asks for documentation readable by people and by machines, machine-readable metadata (schema.org, DCAT, Croissant are named), stable identifiers, APIs next to bulk files, and it discusses knowledge graphs.
findings.lesson: The first official text that treats a language model as a reader of open data. Its core demand is that the meaning of each variable be carried in machine-readable form next to the data, not in a PDF codebook.
findings.verified: NOT verified in this run: commerce.gov returned HTTP 403 on three URLs and search was unavailable. Everything in this entry is recalled from memory; check the URL and the content before citing.

findings.title: Overture Maps: versioned GeoParquet releases with a STAC pointer to 'latest'
findings.what: Data is published as GeoParquet on object storage with Hive partitions (`s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-10-21.0/theme=places/type=place/*`). A STAC catalog (https://stac.overturemaps.org/catalog.json) carries a `latest` field that DuckDB can read to avoid hardcoded paths, and a `latest.ddb` DuckDB file holds one view per feature type. Access is through a Python CLI (`overturemaps download --bbox ... --type=building`) or plain DuckDB SQL. No MCP and no mention of agents.
findings.lesson: An agent-usable publisher without any agent-specific work: immutable dated releases, one small machine-readable pointer to the current release, and a ready DuckDB file of views. A `latest` pointer and a views file are cheap additions that make queries reproducible.
findings.verified: Read the page through WebFetch. Release cadence and the Azure mirror are not on this page.

patterns: Publishers that built an agent interface converge on the same small set of verbs (search or list --> describe or metadata --> fetch rows or observations), with 4 to 10 tools: Data Commons, World Bank Data360, data.gouv.fr, Census Bureau, Wikidata.

A resolver from names to codes is treated as a first-class tool, because agents guess identifiers wrongly: `resolve-geography-fips` (Census), `data360_find_codelist_value` and `get_disaggregation` (World Bank), `search_items` / `search_properties` (Wikidata), `search_indicators` (Data Commons).

Workflow guidance is shipped with the data layer, not left to the client: skills as MCP resources (Data Commons), a system prompt as a resource (World Bank), 'use when' notes and workflow notes in tool descriptions (Wikidata, data.gouv.fr), an MCP prompt (Census).

Outputs are bounded by default and detail is opt-in: 20 rows per page (data.gouv.fr), 10 rows from SPARQL (Wikidata), `select_fields` on metadata (World Bank), short statements versus full statement values (Wikidata).

Hosts of bulk data rely on Parquet at predictable, versioned paths plus DuckDB, with no agent-specific protocol or with a CLI: Hugging Face (`hf://`, `hf datasets sql --format json`), Overture (dated releases, STAC `latest`, `latest.ddb`), Our World in Data (one URL scheme per chart with CSV, metadata and README).

The guidelines demand the same list: a machine-readable data dictionary with units, provenance, licence, update schedule and versioned schemas, known biases and non-recommended uses, open columnar formats, an API next to bulk files (UK GDS/DSIT 2026, ESIP checklist, Commerce 2025 from memory, ODI framework, Croissant 1.1).

Guidelines written for model training (ESIP, Croissant, Bridge2AI) and guidelines written for agents (UK 2026, which names MCP) differ on grain: the UK text asks to keep fine-grained data and to document what each grain supports, and says aggregated tables are not enough.

National statistical offices are uneven: France, the US Census Bureau and the World Bank have public MCP code, while Statistics Canada's developer page (modified 2026-09-11) and sdmx.org offer SDMX services and only a general 'AI ready' vision statement.
disagreements: Many narrow tools versus one generic tool: Data Commons, World Bank and data.gouv.fr expose 6 to 10 typed tools, while the Hugging Face MCP server now says most tasks are done with a single file-system tool (`hf_fs`), and HF also offers SQL through its CLI.

Free query language versus fixed parameters: Wikidata gives the agent `execute_sparql` and Hugging Face gives DuckDB SQL; Data Commons, World Bank, Census and data.gouv.fr give only parameterised fetches, which is safer and less expressive (no joins, no aggregation on the server).
Hosted remote endpoint versus local server: data.gouv.fr, Data Commons and Wikidata run a public HTTP endpoint; the Census Bureau asks the user to run Docker with a local PostgreSQL database.

Which metadata standard: the US Commerce guidance (from memory) and the ODI point to Croissant and schema.org; the UK guidance names only DCAT, Dublin Core and its own GDS schema; statistical agencies stay with SDMX. None of them names Frictionless, as far as I read.

Is an agent-specific interface needed at all: Overture and Our World in Data publish no MCP server in the pages I read and are still easy for a coding agent to use, because paths, formats and metadata are predictable.

Coverage limits of this run: web search was unavailable (the session budget was exhausted), so I fetched known URLs only. Not checked: Kaggle MCP (page needs JavaScript), data.europa.eu, opendata.swiss / LINDAS, Eurostat, IMF, OECD, UN, ONS, Source Cooperative details, NIH Bridge2AI criteria (abstract only), NASA and NOAA standards. I found no evidence for or against agent work at these publishers; absence here means not checked.
results.for_adele: Adele's shape (Parquet + DuckDB + descriptor + CLI with list, describe, query, pull + SKILL.md) matches what Hugging Face, Overture and the public MCP servers converged on. Gaps to consider: (1) a `search` or `resolve` verb over codes and labels (place, variable, category values), the tool that every publisher added; (2) descriptor fields taken from the UK and ESIP checklists: preliminary versus final values, known gaps and biases, non-recommended uses, processing notes, next update, ready citation, schema version; (3) bounded output by default and metadata by field; (4) a `latest` pointer with dated snapshots; (5) optional Croissant export, generated from the Frictionless descriptor. The Commerce and ODI details are unverified in this run.

findings.title: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, "Large Datasets and Structured Databases: Claude Code for Economists" (part 4 of a series)
findings.what: An economist had Claude Code build a mortgage panel (HMDA 2007-2024): 291M rows, about 70 GB of CSV converted to about 6 GB of Parquet, queried with DuckDB, no pandas on the full data. The central device is a `metadata` table inside the .duckdb file (column name, description, type, valid values with code meanings, year coverage), so that a new session runs `SELECT * FROM metadata` and needs no explanation again. Pipeline is plain scripts (download, convert, harmonize, build_db) plus a saved plan file. Reported problems: a sub-agent ignored the "stay in this directory" rule, the delimiter differed from the API documentation, FIPS codes were inconsistent, a break in identifiers in 2018 produced an artificial dip, and some downloads ran as inline curl and were not reproducible.
findings.lesson: This is the closest published twin of Adele at the scale of one person: Parquet + DuckDB + a machine-readable description per column, stored next to the data so that it survives context compaction and handoffs. The description must carry valid values, code meanings and coverage per year, and the known breaks in the series (format eras, identifier changes), because those caused the real errors. Require scripts for every fetch.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page (via WebFetch summary): stack, numbers, metadata table, list of failures. Published 2026-04-05.

findings.title: Anthropic data team, "How Anthropic enables self-service data analytics with Claude"
findings.what: Not small scale, but the most detailed report of failures that I found. The team states that analytics accuracy is a problem of context and verification, not of code generation. Stack: few governed canonical datasets, a semantic layer, lineage, a knowledge skill that routes to about 30 curated reference files per domain (grain, exclusions, gotchas, routing triggers), a runbook skill, offline evals and a provenance footer on each answer. Numbers: at most 21% accuracy on their evals without skills, above 95% with them; accuracy drifted from about 95% to about 65% in one month until documentation was maintained in the same PR as the data model (about 90% of data-model PRs now include a skill change). Failed: metric definitions generated by an LLM (net negative), raw access to thousands of past queries (under 1 point), repeated refinement of docs (three iterations in a row were net negative because docs got longer), a cheaper reviewer model.
findings.lesson: Short curated reference files that state grain, exclusions and gotchas do most of the work; more text is not better. Descriptions decay fast, so generate or update them in the same step that changes the data. Let the model draft descriptions, but a human owns definitions. Keep a small fixed set of question/answer pairs to detect drift. The authors say the heavier process may be unnecessary for simple setups.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page (via WebFetch summary), published 2026-06-03. It is a vendor engineering blog (Anthropic writing about Claude), so the numbers are self-reported and not independently checked.

findings.title: nao Labs context benchmarks: "What Context Has the Most Impact on Analytics Agent Performance?" and the semantic layer follow-up
findings.what: A small ablation by a vendor of an open-source analytics agent (nao, Apache 2.0, about 2k stars, context as files produced by `nao sync`). 40 question/SQL pairs on 12 tables, 8 context configurations, 3 runs each, scored by exact diff of the result data. Reported ranking: a hand-written rules.md (join keys, grain, metric definitions, exclusions, gotchas) helped most; context as files beat schema discovery through MCP (at about 2x tokens); 10 sample rows per table beat column profiling once rules existed; exposing only the clean layer helped; adding the full dbt repository reduced reliability. Best configuration reached only 45%. The follow-up (https://getnao.io/blog/semantic-layer-impact-analytics-agent/) found that semantic YAML added to the context changed nothing, and that forcing queries through a metrics store gave fewer wrong answers but much lower coverage, about 3x the time and 4x the tool calls.
findings.lesson: For a dozen tables, the order of investment is: expose only clean tables --> schema with column descriptions --> about 10 sample rows --> one short file of rules and gotchas. A formal semantic layer is not the first thing to build. Adele's descriptor already covers the first three; the missing piece is the free-text gotchas per dataset.
findings.verified: Both posts read on the primary pages (via WebFetch summary). Per-configuration numbers are in charts that the fetch did not return; only 45% and the relative statements are confirmed. Vendor source, unnamed model, 40 questions with 3 runs: this is a small sample, so differences of a few points between configurations are within run-to-run noise and only the large effects (rules.md, full dbt repo) deserve trust. A third-party dev.to post cites the same work as 17% --> 86%; the nao blog index says 45% --> 86%; I could not reconcile the 17%.

findings.title: Simon Willison, NICAR 2026 workshop "Coding agents for data analysis" (handout) + Showboat
findings.what: A three-hour workshop for data journalists (announcement: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Mar/16/coding-agents-for-data-analysis/). Stack: SQLite, sqlite-utils, Datasette, Codex and Claude Code in Codespaces; the whole room spent $23 of tokens. The pattern is thin: load a CSV into SQLite, let the agent query it through a CLI (`sqlite-utils`, or `dclient` for a remote Datasette), and tell the agent to learn each tool with `--help`. The agent starts from `select sql from sqlite_master`. Showboat (https://github.com/simonw/showboat, about 1.3k stars) records each command and its output in a Markdown file that `showboat verify` can re-run. The handout lists what to check: re-run queries yourself, the agent may misread what a column means, spikes may be reporting deadlines.
findings.lesson: The small-scale consensus interface is a CLI whose `--help` is the documentation, plus SQL. Two things the handout names as the real risks are exactly what a descriptor should prevent: wrong reading of a column, and artifacts of how data is reported. A replayable log of the queries behind an answer is cheap and gives auditability.
findings.verified: Read the announcement post, the pages asking-questions.html and exploring-data.html, and the Showboat README (via WebFetch summary). The other handout sections (cleaning, visualizations, scraping) were not read.

findings.title: Simon Willison, DSPy evaluation of the Datasette Agent prompts (and the Datasette Agent release)
findings.what: Datasette Agent (2026-05-21, https://simonwillison.net/2026/May/21/datasette-agent/) is a plugin that answers questions by writing read-only SQL against SQLite; the demo runs on a cheap small model (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite). An evaluation harness built with DSPy then ran the real tools and prompts on an auto-generated gold set. The main finding: the schema listing in the prompt showed only table names while the prompt advised against calling `describe_table` when the information was already available. Baseline traces showed the model guessing column names (page_count, o.order_id, first_name) and looping on errors. The proposed fix is to include column names in the listing or soften the advice.
findings.lesson: What `list` prints decides whether the agent guesses. If the cheap overview omits column names, the agent invents them instead of calling `describe`. Put column names (and units) in the first thing the agent sees, and check that SKILL.md advice matches what the output really contains. Traces of real runs reveal this faster than reasoning about the prompt.
findings.verified: Read both posts on the primary site (via WebFetch summary). The July post is a short link post; no accuracy numbers are given there (they would be in the linked repo, which I did not open).

findings.title: Vercel, "We removed 80% of our agent's tools" (d0)
findings.what: Vercel's internal text-to-SQL agent went from 17 specialized tools (schema lookup, validation, error recovery, hand-coded retrieval) to essentially two: run bash in a sandbox, and run SQL. The semantic layer (Cube) is a directory of YAML, Markdown and JSON files that the agent reads with grep, cat, find and ls. On 5 benchmark queries: success 4/5 --> 5/5, 274.8 s --> 77.4 s, about 102k --> 61k tokens, about 12 --> 7 steps. Their own caveat: with poor names or undocumented joins, "You'll just get faster bad queries."
findings.lesson: Descriptions as plain files that the agent can grep, plus one query command, beat a wide tool surface. This supports Adele's four-verb CLI, and it argues for also leaving the descriptors on disk as files (not only behind `describe`). The precondition is the quality of the descriptions.
findings.verified: Read on the primary page (via WebFetch summary), published 2025-12-22. Vendor blog that promotes Vercel products; the benchmark has only 5 queries, so 80% versus 100% is one query of difference and is an anecdote, not a measurement.

findings.title: marimo, "marimo pair: letting agents use notebooks as a tool" + Hacker News thread
findings.what: marimo first connected agents through a read-only MCP server with fixed tools (list_cells, read_cell). It failed in a specific way: "The MCP tools worked for questions we had anticipated", and each new need required a new endpoint. They replaced it with a skill plus a CLI that runs arbitrary Python in the live kernel (scratchpad calls), and a transactional API to commit cells, where the runtime rejects invalid edits with specific errors. The skill tells the agent to run `help(cm)` so that the API documents itself. In the HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47678844) the maintainer confirms the move from discrete MCP tools to a bash script; others (Posit's t-kalinowski, agentnb, replsh) converge on "one REPL tool".
findings.lesson: Give the agent a general language (SQL or Python) over the data instead of a menu of fixed views; enforce rules in the tool and return actionable errors instead of writing the rules in the skill; keep the skill short and let the tool describe itself at run time. Separate scratch exploration from work that is kept.
findings.verified: Read the blog post (2026-07-20, Trevor Manz), the docs page and the HN thread (via WebFetch summary). Engineering blog of the vendor of the tool.

findings.title: Kevin Schaul (Washington Post), "AI data journalism" write-up on consolidating federal AI inventories
findings.what: A data journalist used Claude Code (Opus 4.5) and Codex to find, download and merge the AI use-case inventories of federal agencies, which come in different formats and column schemes, for a published story. The one-shot prompt (find + download + merge) hit the usage limit after about 10 minutes of web search with nothing saved. What worked: one step at a time, a download script driven by a CSV of URLs, a merge script refined iteratively, idempotent reruns, reading all the code. His rule: he would not trust an LLM to read the data directly, but is comfortable with AI writing code that can be audited and rerun.
findings.lesson: Newsroom practice puts the trust boundary at code, not at the model's reading of rows: answers must come from a query or script that a human can rerun. Fetching must be scripted, incremental and idempotent, with progress written to files. Harmonizing heterogeneous public files is where agents save the most time.
findings.verified: Read on the author's own blog (via WebFetch summary); also read the secondary coverage at mediacopilot.ai. Related but only abstract read: Data2Story (arXiv:2606.11176), a multi-agent system where an inspector links each number to data or code and a verifier re-executes it; 18 articles, 53 raters.

findings.title: Data Tripper, "Context Engineering for Analytics Engineers" (mining query logs into a join registry)
findings.what: An analytics engineer parsed hundreds of thousands of production queries with sqlglot (built with Claude Code) and produced three small files kept in the docs folder of the dbt repo: a `join-registry.yml` (tables, keys, join type, frequency, risk of orphans), a library of slow patterns with measured penalty (NOT IN with subquery 4.18x slower, SELECT * 2.08x), and a mapping of canonical names. Before, about 4 in 10 agent queries needed fixes and agents invented field names; after, the author reports far fewer corrections and no more "column does not exist" errors (no measured rate given).
findings.lesson: The most common concrete failures are invented columns and wrong join paths. A small file of verified joins (which key, which grain, what breaks) removes them. For Adele, which has no query history, the equivalent is to write by hand the few valid joins between datasets (shared keys, time zone, resolution) in the descriptors.
findings.verified: Read on the primary Substack page (via WebFetch summary), published 2026-02-23. The author is pseudonymous and the improvement is reported without a measured after-rate. It contradicts in part Anthropic's finding that raw query history barely helps; the difference is that here the history is distilled into a small curated file.

findings.title: Tim Hiebenthal, "DuckBrain" (Hands-On Data) and Karpathy's "LLM Wiki" gist
findings.what: Two personal-scale knowledge stacks with the same position. DuckBrain: about 300 lines of Python, 4 MCP tools, DuckDB full-text search over an Obsidian vault, built in about 3 hours; Markdown files are the single source of truth, no vectors; the author rejected tools that copy files into Qdrant, Supabase or Milvus (about 600 MB of dependencies, stale indexes from file watchers). Karpathy's gist (https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f, 2026-04-04): raw sources that are never modified, a wiki of Markdown pages that the LLM maintains, a schema file (CLAUDE.md), an index.md with one line per page that the LLM reads first, an append-only log.md, and a periodic lint for stale or contradictory pages; no embeddings at moderate scale.
findings.lesson: At personal scale people converge on: plain files in git that a human can read and correct, an index with one line per item read first, keyword search instead of vectors, DuckDB to query files in place. An append-only log and a lint pass (stale coverage, description versus actual schema) transfer directly to a dataset catalog.
findings.verified: Read both primary pages (via WebFetch summary). DuckBrain's author admits that he did not test most alternatives in depth. A third project, personal-db (https://github.com/intelc/personal-db, 3 stars), shows the same shape for personal structured data: one SQLite file, one manifest.yaml + schema.sql + ingest.py per source, validation before sync, single writer; README only.

findings.title: Skill collections of researchers and journalists (AERS for empirical social science, claude-skills-journalism)
findings.what: Research and newsroom communities package practice as skills, not as data infrastructure. AERS (about 5k stars, maintained by CoPaper.AI with Stanford REAP) lists 78 collections with 1,151 skills for economics and social science: Stata and R workflows, causal inference, replication audits, and a few thin wrappers for data access (Kaggle CLI, SEC EDGAR via edgartools, OpenAlex). claude-skills-journalism (https://github.com/jamditis/claude-skills-journalism, 452 stars) has a DuckDB/polars pipeline skill, a catalog of free APIs, and a hook that flags data stories without a methodology section.
findings.lesson: In these communities almost nobody publishes a described, queryable data layer; they publish procedures and wrappers around other people's APIs. A small server with curated descriptors is rarer than skills, and the useful idea to borrow is the enforcement by hook (an answer must state its sources and method).
findings.verified: Only the two README pages were read (via WebFetch summary). Star counts and skill counts are from those pages; the About text of AERS claims "23,000+" skills while the README counts 1,151. I did not read individual SKILL.md files, so the quality is unknown.

findings.title: Rakesh Therani, "How to Build a Self-Learning Agentic Analytics System on ClickHouse"
findings.what: A long build guide (about 1,200 lines of code claimed) that compiles the practice of others into one layout: context as Markdown in git (rules.md, metrics.md, tables/*.md with physical layout and gotchas, skills/*.md, memory/corrections.yaml), three tools only (read_context, execute_sql, explain_query), `execute_sql` refuses to run until the context was read, requests for a context file that does not exist are logged as a signal of what to document next, 40+ golden questions gate changes, and a daily rerun detects drift.
findings.lesson: Two cheap mechanisms are worth copying: log what the agent asked for and did not find (it tells you which description is missing), and make the tool nudge or force a `describe` before the first `query` on a dataset. The rest is sized for a company.
findings.verified: Read only the first 100,000 of about 193,000 characters (via WebFetch summary). It is a secondary compilation: its numbers for Ramp, OpenAI, Gorgias and Vercel are given without links and I did not verify them, except Vercel and Anthropic, which match the primary posts.

patterns: Parquet or SQLite files + an embedded SQL engine + plain scripts is the default stack at small scale; nobody at this scale runs a warehouse or a vector store (Goldsmith-Pinkham, Willison NICAR, DuckBrain, personal-db).

The description of the data is stored next to the data in a form that the agent reads with ordinary tools (a metadata table, Markdown or YAML files, an index read first), and it must state grain, units, code meanings, coverage and known breaks (Goldsmith-Pinkham, Anthropic, nao, Vercel, Karpathy).

Short curated context beats exhaustive context: a rules or gotchas file and about 10 sample rows help most, while full repositories, raw query history and ever longer docs are neutral or harmful (nao, Anthropic, Vercel).

Few general tools (a shell or CLI with good --help, plus SQL or Python) replace many fixed tools, and several teams moved from MCP endpoints to that shape after the fixed views proved too narrow (marimo, Vercel, Willison, HN thread).

The most frequent concrete failures are invented column names, wrong joins or grain, and misreading a column or a reporting artifact; they come from what the overview omits (Willison DSPy evaluation, Data Tripper, NICAR handout, Goldsmith-Pinkham).

Trust is placed in code that can be rerun and audited, not in the model reading rows; practitioners want a replayable record of queries and a provenance line per answer (Schaul, Showboat, Anthropic, Data2Story).

Descriptions decay within weeks unless they are updated in the same step as the data, and a small fixed set of questions with known answers is the only way people detect it (Anthropic, nao, the ClickHouse guide).

Agents are good and cheap at the ingestion work (download, convert, harmonize heterogeneous public files) when it is done step by step with scripts and saved progress; one-shot runs and inline commands failed (Schaul, Goldsmith-Pinkham).
disagreements: Semantic layer: Vercel and the Anthropic team place a semantic layer at the center, while nao's small benchmark found that semantic YAML added nothing over a rules file and that a metrics store cut coverage at 3x the latency. The setups differ (large governed organizations versus 12 tables, a layer built in days), and nao sells a competing approach.

Query history as context: Anthropic measured under 1 point of gain from raw access to thousands of past queries; Data Tripper reports a large gain from the same raw material once distilled into a small join registry. Compatible reading: structure helps, access does not. Neither result was replicated.

MCP versus CLI and files: marimo and Vercel moved away from fixed MCP tools, yet DuckBrain and personal-db at personal scale still choose MCP (for reach across Claude Desktop, Cursor and others), and nao found that rules.md + a warehouse MCP did almost as well as files. The real variable seems to be general versus fixed tools, not the protocol.

Who writes the descriptions: Anthropic found LLM-generated metric definitions net negative and wants humans to own definitions; Karpathy's wiki and Goldsmith-Pinkham's metadata table are written by the agent. No one measured this at small scale.

Strength of evidence: almost every number here is self-reported on tiny samples (Vercel 5 queries, nao 40 questions with 3 runs) or by vendors. With 5 queries, one query changes the success rate by 20 points; with 40 questions, differences of a few points between configurations cannot be told apart from run-to-run variation. Only the large effects should guide design.

Coverage gap of this search: the web search budget of the session ran out after the first round. I found nothing verifiable for quant or finance shops, for Evidence, Observable or Hex with agents, or for Reddit threads; the absence of findings there reflects the interrupted search, not the field.
results.for_adele:
The design matches what individuals converge on (Parquet, DuckDB, per-dataset descriptor, small CLI, skill). Changes that the evidence supports:

1. `list` should print column names and units, not only dataset names; otherwise agents guess columns.
2. Add to each descriptor a short hand-written "gotchas" block: grain, code meanings, series breaks, reporting artifacts, valid joins to other datasets.
3. Keep descriptors also as plain files that the agent can grep.
4. Keep the skill short; put rules in the CLI as specific errors and in `--help`.
5. Regenerate coverage, freshness and sample rows on every fetch.
6. Log queries (provenance) and failed `describe` lookups.
7. Keep 20 to 40 questions with known answers to detect drift.

Skip a semantic layer and vectors.

findings.title: Supabase MCP data leak demonstration (General Analysis) and Simon Willison's reading of it as a "lethal trifecta"
findings.what: Security researchers (8 July 2025) built a support-ticket app on Supabase with row-level security enabled. An attacker wrote hidden instructions in a ticket message. When a developer asked Cursor (through the Supabase MCP server) to show the latest ticket, the assistant read the message as a command, selected the private `integration_tokens` table and inserted its content into the ticket thread. The assistant ran as `service_role`, which bypasses row-level security by design. Willison (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jul/6/supabase-mcp-lethal-trifecta/) notes that this single server supplied all three conditions: private data, untrusted content, and a channel to send data out.
findings.lesson: Text stored in rows is an instruction channel for whatever agent reads the rows. Row-level security does not help if the agent connects with a role above it. The mitigation that works is structural: remove one of the three conditions (here: read-only role, and keep secrets out of the reachable schema), not filtering.
findings.verified: Read both primary pages (General Analysis post and Willison's post). The General Analysis page states that it was reviewed on 21 October 2026 without rerunning the test against the current server.

findings.title: Supabase: "Defense in Depth for MCP Servers" (vendor response to the leak)
findings.what: Supabase lists what it added: read-only mode, scoping to a single project, feature groups that restrict which tools the model can call, wrapping of query results with a warning that tells the model not to follow instructions found in the data, experiments with LLM classifiers, and a recommendation to keep manual approval of each tool call. Its four recommended practices: use non-production data, keep manual approval on, limit capabilities, monitor and log every MCP query. It states that guardrails reduced the risk and did not eliminate it, and that prompt injection stays its top concern even in read-only mode.
findings.lesson: A vendor with every incentive to say "fixed" says instead that wrapping and classifiers are not sufficient. What it treats as mandatory is boring: read-only by default, narrow scope, a log of every query, and no production secrets within reach of the agent.
findings.verified: Read the primary page. It is a vendor blog, but it is an engineering response with admissions of limits, not marketing. The claim of zero reported customer incidents is the vendor's own.

findings.title: Datadog Security Labs: SQL injection in the reference Postgres MCP server (read-only bypass)
findings.what: Anthropic's reference server `@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres` (v0.6.2, archived, about 21,000 weekly npm downloads) enforced read-only access by wrapping each query in `BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY` ... `ROLLBACK`. The Node `pg` client accepts several statements separated by semicolons, so an input that starts with `COMMIT;` ends the read-only transaction and the rest runs with write access (the example is `DROP SCHEMA`). Because connections are pooled, the injected SQL can also change session state (e.g. `statement_timeout` of 1 ms) and break the queries of other users. The fix (in the Zed fork) uses prepared statements, which accept a single statement, and destroys the connection after use.
findings.lesson: "Read-only" enforced by the application around the query is not read-only. Enforce it below the query: a database role or file opened without write permission, one statement per call, and no session state shared between calls.
findings.verified: Read the primary page in full (summary by the fetch tool). Download numbers are those reported in the article.

findings.title: DuckDB documentation: "Securing DuckDB" (running untrusted SQL)
findings.what: The official checklist for untrusted SQL: `SET allowed_directories = [...]` then `SET enable_external_access = false` (blocks ATTACH, COPY, read_csv/read_parquet on arbitrary paths and URLs); disable automatic install and load of extensions and community extensions; set `threads`, `memory_limit`, `max_temp_directory_size`; finish with `SET lock_configuration = true` so that the query cannot undo the settings. The page states that DuckDB has no built-in query timeout ("implement strict query timeouts at the application level") and that these settings are "not a substitute for proper sandboxing".
findings.lesson: With DuckDB, a free-form `query` command is by default a file reader and an HTTP client (`read_parquet('https://...')`, `COPY ... TO`). An agent-facing DuckDB endpoint needs the lock-down sequence in a fixed order, a read-only connection, and a timeout that the wrapper process enforces, because the engine has none.
findings.verified: Read the primary docs page (DuckDB 2.0 docs, reached through a redirect from the stable URL). SQL statements quoted from the page via the fetch tool.

findings.title: Meta: "Agents Rule of Two" (and Willison's "lethal trifecta")
findings.what: Meta's rule: until prompt injection can be reliably detected, an agent session should hold at most two of three properties: [A] processes untrustworthy inputs, [B] accesses sensitive systems or private data, [C] changes state or communicates externally. If all three are needed, the agent must not run autonomously (human approval or a fresh session). Willison's version (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/) is the same triple restricted to data theft, with the remark that a filter that catches 95% of attacks is "very much a failing grade" in security.
findings.lesson: This is the design check that experienced teams apply to a data layer: classify every dataset as trusted or untrusted content, and every consumer session by what else it can read and where it can send. A data layer of public data supplies property [A] to an agent that usually already has [B] and [C].
findings.verified: Read both primary pages. Meta's post states its own limits (does not cover hallucination or excess privilege).

findings.title: LinkedIn SQL Bot: "Practical text-to-SQL for data analytics"
findings.what: An internal multi-agent text-to-SQL system inside LinkedIn's DARWIN platform, used by hundreds of employees. Trust mechanisms: domain experts certified hundreds of tables with mandatory descriptions; deprecated tables are removed automatically through DataHub flags; validators check that tables and fields exist and run EXPLAIN before the query is shown; access is checked per dataset against the user's groups. Evaluation: 130+ benchmark questions over 10 product areas, scored by experts and an LLM judge; about 60% of questions have several accepted answers, and without them recall was under-reported by 10 to 15%.
findings.lesson: Three mandatory pieces: a curated set of certified datasets (not the whole lake), deterministic validators that use information that the model did not have (catalog, EXPLAIN), and a small benchmark with several accepted answers per question that experts review every quarter.
findings.verified: Read the primary engineering blog. Satisfaction figures (about 95% rate accuracy "Passes" or above) come from an internal survey, so they measure opinion, not correctness.

findings.title: Uber QueryGPT
findings.what: Uber's natural-language-to-SQL service (about 1.2 million interactive queries per month on the platform; about 300 daily users in the limited release). Queries are scoped by "workspaces" (12 curated sets of tables and SQL samples per business domain); the user confirms or edits the selected tables before generation. Evaluation uses golden question-to-SQL pairs built from real logs, with per-question metrics (intent, table overlap, does it run, does it return rows, similarity to the golden SQL). The authors do not act on changes of about 5% between runs because the model output varies from run to run, and they say hallucinated tables and columns are not fully solved.
findings.lesson: Golden SQL built from real logs is the standard regression test, and teams read it with a tolerance: a difference smaller than the run-to-run variation (here about 5 points) is treated as no difference. A human checkpoint on table selection is cheaper than verifying the final SQL.
findings.verified: Read the primary engineering blog. The post dates from 2024, before the period of interest, but it is the most explicit primary account of the evaluation method.

findings.title: Snowflake Cortex Analyst: Verified Query Repository, role-based execution, and agent traces
findings.what: A `verified_queries` section in the semantic model YAML holds entries with `name`, `question`, `sql`, optional `verified_by`, `verified_at` and `use_as_onboarding_question`. When a new question resembles a stored one, the stored SQL is used to generate the answer, and the API response says which verified query was used. Generated SQL runs in the caller's warehouse under the caller's role (the model sees only metadata). Agent runs are traced per turn (planning, tool calls, SQL execution, user feedback) into an event table whose entries cannot be modified; reading full inputs and outputs needs a separate privilege.
findings.lesson: The verified query is a small, portable format: question, SQL, who verified it, when. Three properties recur across platforms: the answer discloses whether it came from a verified query, the SQL runs with the identity of the human caller, and the log of agent queries is append-only with access to its content restricted.
findings.verified: Read three primary docs pages (verified query repository, Cortex Analyst overview, Cortex Agents monitoring at https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/cortex-agents-monitor). Vendor docs: they describe the features, not how well they work.

findings.title: Databricks Genie benchmarks
findings.what: Each Genie agent can hold up to 500 benchmark questions, each ideally with 2 to 4 phrasings and one gold SQL.
