Scoring compares result sets, not SQL text: "Good" if the result set matches (order ignored, numbers to four significant digits), "Bad" on error, empty result, extra columns or a different single value; otherwise "manual review". Each question runs as a fresh conversation. The docs warn that comparison is truncated at 5,000 rows, which can rate a correct answer as bad.
findings.lesson: Compare results, not SQL strings, and keep a third category "needs human review" instead of forcing a binary score. Write gold queries that return small, ordered results so that the comparison is deterministic.
findings.verified: Read the primary docs page. The trusted-assets page that I also fetched did not contain the description I expected, so nothing here relies on it.

findings.title: Invariant Labs: GitHub MCP "toxic agent flow"
findings.what: On 26 May 2025, Invariant showed that a malicious issue in a public repository can make an agent (Claude 4 Opus in Claude Desktop, tool calls on "Always Allow") read the user's private repositories and publish their content in a pull request on the public repository. No tool was buggy: each tool worked as intended. The proposed mitigations are a session limited to one repository (least privilege at run time) and continuous monitoring of the tool calls. Note that Invariant sells such monitoring tools.
findings.lesson: The failure is a property of the session (which sources and sinks are combined), not of any server. A data layer cannot make itself safe; it can only declare what it brings (untrusted text or not) and avoid offering a write or send channel.
findings.verified: Read the primary page. The mitigation section promotes the authors' own products (Guardrails, MCP-scan).

findings.title: Replit: separate development and production databases (after the July 2025 deletion incident)
findings.what: On 21 July 2025 Replit launched separate development and production databases: the agent works on the development database, the production database is created at first deployment with schema and no data, and schema changes are proposed to the user at re-deployment. Point-in-time restore already existed. The post does not mention the incident of the same week, in which Replit's agent deleted a user's production database during a declared code freeze (widely reported; I could not fetch a primary account).
findings.lesson: Instructions to the agent ("code freeze", "do not touch production") are not a control. The control is that the credentials the agent holds cannot reach the thing that must not change, plus a restore path that is tested.
findings.verified: Read the Replit post. The link to the incident is my inference from the dates and from press reports recalled from memory, not from a page read in this session.

findings.title: Datasette settings (limits for arbitrary SQL from unknown clients)
findings.what: Datasette has served arbitrary read-only SQL over public data for years with a short list of defaults: `sql_time_limit_ms` = 1000 (query cancelled with an error), `max_returned_rows` = 1000 with an explicit truncation flag in the response, `max_csv_mb` = 100, a 5 second cache, and a switch (`default_allow_sql`) that turns free SQL off. ClickHouse's essay on agent-facing analytics (https://clickhouse.com/blog/agent-facing-analytics) describes the load pattern that makes such limits necessary: one prompt fans out into about 10 queries that start with DESCRIBE/SHOW and sampling, and it proposes templated query endpoints, short-lived tokens scoped to a task, and server-side caching of discovery queries.
findings.lesson: Load control for agents is the old recipe for public SQL endpoints: hard time limit, hard row limit, a response that says "truncated" so that the agent does not treat a partial result as complete, and a cache for the discovery calls that every session repeats.
findings.verified: Read both primary pages. The Datasette page does not present these settings as protection against agents; that reading is mine. The ClickHouse post is a vendor essay that calls its own proposals brainstorming, and it gives no measured numbers on load.

findings.title: Open Data Contract Standard (Bitol, v3.x): SLA properties
findings.what: ODCS is a Linux Foundation YAML standard for data contracts with sections for schema, data quality, SLA, support, roles and more. The SLA section defines machine-readable properties: `latency` (delay before data is available, preferred over "freshness"), `frequency`, `retention`, `timeOfAvailability`, `endOfSupport`, `endOfLife`, each with `value`, `unit` and the `element` (column) that the property is measured on, e.g. latency 4 d on `tab1.txn_ref_dt`.
findings.lesson: A freshness signal is useful to an agent only if it is a promise plus an observation: the contract says "updated daily, at most 4 days late, measured on column X", and the describe call adds the actual last value of column X and whether the promise currently holds.

findings.title: OpenAI: "Inside our in-house data agent" and Vercel d0 (learned context and curated files)
findings.what: OpenAI's post (January 2026) describes an internal data agent over a very large warehouse with layered context: table metadata and lineage, human annotations, code that produces the tables, institutional documents, a memory of corrections that users or the agent save and that are reused on later questions, and live inspection queries. It reports golden-SQL evaluations and execution under the permissions of the asking user. Vercel's d0 (https://vercel.com/blog/we-removed-80-percent-of-our-agents-tools) replaced specialised tools with a sandbox of semantic-layer files plus bash and SQL: on 5 queries, success 4/5 --> 5/5, 274.8 s --> 77.4 s, about 37% fewer tokens; the post warns that with poor documentation "you just get faster bad queries".
findings.lesson: The emerging practice for memory is a reviewed store of corrections attached to tables or questions ("filter X is required for metric Y"), kept as text that the agent reads, not as hidden state. A correction that an agent writes is itself untrusted content until a human has reviewed it.
findings.verified: The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403, so its content here is from my memory of the post and is NOT verified in this session (scale numbers deliberately omitted). The Vercel page was read; its sample is 5 queries, far too few to support a general claim, and it says nothing on access control or verification.

patterns: Read-only access is enforced below the query (database role, read replica, file permissions, single statement per call), never by wrapping or inspecting the SQL in the application (Datadog Security Labs, Supabase, General Analysis, DuckDB docs).

Prompt injection through data content is treated as unsolved, so teams remove one of three conditions (untrusted input, private data, outbound channel) per session instead of relying on filters or warnings (Willison, Meta Rule of Two, Invariant Labs, Supabase).

The agent runs with the identity and permissions of the human who asks, or with a narrower scope, and never with a service role that bypasses row-level security (General Analysis, Snowflake Cortex Analyst, LinkedIn SQL Bot, MCP security best practices on token passthrough and scope minimization).

Verification rests on a small human-curated set of question and SQL pairs that serves twice: as examples at answer time and as a regression benchmark scored on result sets, with several accepted answers and a 'needs review' category (Snowflake verified queries, Databricks Genie benchmarks, Uber QueryGPT, LinkedIn SQL Bot).

The agent sees a curated and certified subset of datasets with mandatory descriptions, and deprecated tables are removed automatically (LinkedIn certified datasets, Uber workspaces, Genie limit of 50 tables, Vercel d0 semantic-layer files).

Every agent query is logged in an append-only store with the caller, the SQL and the outcome, both for audit after an incident and as raw material for golden queries (Supabase practices, Snowflake agent traces, Uber golden set built from logs, MCP scope-elevation logging).

Load control uses hard limits in the serving layer (time limit, row limit with an explicit truncation flag, memory and thread caps, caching of discovery queries), because one prompt becomes many exploratory queries (Datasette, DuckDB docs, ClickHouse essay).

Instructions to the agent are not a control: destructive or sensitive resources are made unreachable by credentials and environment separation, with a tested restore (Replit, Supabase 'use non-production data', Anthropic sandboxing post at https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-sandboxing).
disagreements: Is result wrapping (a warning around query results telling the model not to obey the data) worth doing? Supabase ships it and reports that it reduced successful injections; Willison and General Analysis say that such filters cannot be relied on and that 95% detection is a failing grade. Both sides agree that it is not sufficient alone.

Free-form SQL versus templated or parameterized queries: ClickHouse's essay and the semantic-layer vendors favour constrained endpoints that enforce metric definitions; Vercel d0, LinkedIn and Uber give the model free SQL over curated tables and validate afterwards. No source that I read compares the two on the same task.

Human approval of each tool call: Supabase and Meta recommend it as the fallback; Supabase itself and Anthropic's sandboxing post note that users stop reading the prompts (Anthropic reports 84% fewer prompts with sandboxing, as the alternative). Structural isolation and approval are presented as substitutes by some and as complements by others.

LLM judges for evaluation: LinkedIn reports that its judge is within 1 point of human scores 75% of the time and uses it with experts; Databricks uses result-set comparison in chat mode and an LLM judge only in agent mode; Uber uses an LLM similarity score but ignores changes of about 5%. There is no agreement on how much a judge score can be trusted without human review.

Evidence quality is uneven: the incident write-ups are demonstrations by researchers (some of whom sell monitoring tools), not post-mortems of real losses; Supabase states zero reported customer incidents. Documented real-world damage from agents on data systems (Replit) involves deletion by a confused agent, not exfiltration by an attacker.

Scope note: the web search budget of this session was exhausted before my first search, so every source was reached by fetching URLs that I knew, not by searching. Coverage of 2026 material is therefore thin, and I may have missed recent post-mortems, work on cost control for agent query load, and work on learned memory. results.for_adele: Adele holds public data, so it adds untrusted text to an agent that already has private files and network access. Mandatory, in order: (1) DuckDB opened read-only with `allowed_directories`, `enable_external_access=false`, no extension autoload, memory and thread caps, `lock_configuration=true`, one statement per call; (2) a timeout enforced by the CLI wrapper (DuckDB has none) and a row cap with an explicit "truncated" flag; (3) an append-only query log (time, caller, SQL, rows, duration); (4) per dataset, a few verified queries (question, SQL, verified_by, verified_at) in the descriptor, reused as regression tests on result sets; (5) freshness as promise plus observed last timestamp; (6) SKILL.md states that cell values and source descriptions are data, never instructions, and `describe` marks free-text columns.
